## How to Make a Barcode: EAN-13, Code 128, UPC and More

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/how-to-make-barcode-ean-13-code-128/
Tool: Barcode Generator (https://biscsindia.com/tools/barcode-generator/)

Quick answer: To make a barcode, choose a format that suits your use, such as Code 128 for internal labels or EAN-13 for retail products, enter the number or text, and download the image. BISCS India’s free Barcode Generator creates barcodes in your browser as PNG or SVG. For retail products, the number itself must be licensed from GS1.

A barcode stores a number or short text as a pattern of bars that a scanner can read in a fraction of a second. To make one, choose the right **format** for your use, enter the data, and download the image. For internal labels, **Code 128** is usually the best choice. For products sold in retail stores, **EAN-13** is the standard in India and most of the world.

The free [Barcode Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/barcode-generator/) creates all the common formats in your browser and downloads them as PNG or SVG, with no sign-up and no uploads.

## Which barcode formats are supported?

| Format | What it encodes | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Code 128 | Any letters, numbers and symbols | SKUs, shipping labels, asset tags, files |
| EAN-13 | 13 digits | Retail products in India and worldwide |
| EAN-8 | 8 digits | Very small retail packs |
| UPC-A | 12 digits | Retail products mainly in the US and Canada |
| Code 39 | Uppercase A–Z, digits, space and - . $ / + % | Older industrial and ID systems |
| ITF-14 | 14 digits | Cartons and outer cases |
| MSI Plessey | Digits | Shelf labels and warehouses |
| Pharmacode | A number from 3 to 131070 | Pharmaceutical packaging control |
| Codabar | Digits and a few symbols | Libraries, blood banks, older systems |

If you are not sure, pick Code 128. It is compact, reads reliably and accepts almost anything you type.

## How to create a barcode with the BISCS tool

1. Open the [Barcode Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/barcode-generator/).
2. Choose the **Type** of barcode. A sample value appears, with a hint describing what that format accepts.
3. Type your own **content**, such as an SKU like `KUR-BLU-M-042` or a 12-digit EAN number.
4. Adjust **bar width**, **height**, **font size** and **quiet zone** (the blank margin).
5. Choose bar and background colours, tick **Show text below** for a human-readable number, or make the background transparent.
6. Download as **PNG** (exported at double resolution) or **SVG** for sharp printing at any size.

If the content is not valid for the chosen format, for example letters in an EAN-13 field, the tool explains what is wrong instead of producing a broken barcode. All drawing happens on your device.

## EAN-13 and the check digit, explained

An EAN-13 number has three parts: a **GS1 prefix** (890 for numbers issued through GS1 India), a **company and product number**, and a final **check digit**.

The check digit lets a scanner catch misreads. To calculate it:

1. Take the first 12 digits, for example `890123456789`.
2. Starting from the rightmost digit, multiply digits alternately by 3 and 1.
3. Add the results. Here the total is 130.
4. The check digit is the amount needed to reach the next multiple of 10. 130 is already a multiple of 10, so the check digit is **0**.

The full number is **8901234567890**. In the generator, you can type just the 12 digits and it adds the check digit for you. If you type all 13, it checks that the last digit is correct, which is a quick way to spot a typo on a product list.

### Do you need GS1 registration?

For goods sold through supermarkets, large retail chains or many online marketplaces, yes. The barcode image is easy to make, but the **number** must be unique worldwide. In India, GS1 India allots EAN numbers to registered companies for a fee. Making up an 890 number risks clashing with another company's product. Check the current registration process and fees on GS1 India's official website.

For goods you sell only in your own shop, or for internal stock, you can use your own numbering with Code 128.

## Practical uses for small businesses

- **Kirana and retail stores:** label loose or self-packed items with your own codes for faster billing.
- **Boutiques and clothing shops:** encode style, colour and size in an SKU like `KUR-BLU-M-042`.
- **Warehouses:** use ITF-14 on cartons and Code 128 on bin locations.
- **Offices and schools:** tag laptops, projectors and library books for audits.
- **Events:** print barcodes on passes for quick check-in.

## Printing tips for barcodes that scan first time

- **Size matters.** Very small barcodes are hard to print sharply. Increase the bar width if your printer struggles.
- **Keep the quiet zone.** Leave clear space on both sides; text or borders too close can stop a scan.
- **Use high contrast.** Black bars on white is safest. Red bars are a common mistake, because many scanners use red light and cannot see them.
- **Use SVG for label software** and design tools, so the bars stay crisp at any size.
- **Test before a big print run,** with the actual scanner or app you will use.
- **Choose matte labels** if glare from glossy stickers causes misreads.

## Common barcode mistakes

- Using EAN-13 for internal stock when Code 128 would be simpler.
- Inventing retail numbers instead of getting them from GS1.
- Duplicating the same code on two different products in your system.
- Stretching a barcode image unevenly, which distorts the bar widths.
- Printing on curved or textured surfaces without testing.
- Forgetting the human-readable text, which staff need when a scan fails.

## Barcode or QR code?

Linear barcodes store a short number and suit billing systems and inventory scanners. QR codes store far more, such as a full website link, Wi-Fi details or a UPI payment address, and can be read by any phone camera. For marketing or payments, use the [QR Code Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/qr-code-generator/). For product labels on a billing counter, stick with a barcode.

When you start selling, the [GST Invoice Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/invoice-generator/) creates proper tax invoices, and the [HSN Code Finder](https://biscsindia.com/tools/hsn-code-finder/) helps you find the right HSN code for each product.

A clear, correctly formatted barcode saves time at every scan. Make yours with the [Barcode Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/barcode-generator/) and test it once before printing in bulk.

Q: Can I sell products in shops with a barcode made here?
A: The generator draws a correct barcode image for any number you enter, but retail barcodes also need a unique, registered number. In India, EAN-13 numbers starting with 890 are allotted by GS1 India to member companies. Large retailers and online marketplaces usually require GS1-registered numbers, so register first and then create the image.

Q: Which barcode type should I use for my own stock?
A: Code 128 is the most flexible choice for internal use. It accepts letters, numbers and symbols, is compact, and almost every scanner reads it. Use it for SKU labels, asset tags, files and library books. Choose EAN or UPC only when a product will be sold through retail systems that expect them.

Q: What is the check digit in an EAN-13 barcode?
A: It is the 13th digit, calculated from the first 12 so that scanners can detect misreads. If you type 12 digits, the generator adds it for you. If you type 13 digits, the last one must be correct or the tool shows an error, which catches typing mistakes.

Q: Why will my barcode not scan after printing?
A: The usual causes are printing too small, bars blurred by a low-quality printer, low contrast colours, or a quiet zone that is too narrow. Print at a larger bar width, use dark bars on a white background, keep empty space on both sides, and test with the scanner you will actually use.

## Base64 Encode and Decode Online: What It Is and When to Use It

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/base64-encode-decode-explained/
Tool: Base64 Encode / Decode (https://biscsindia.com/tools/base64-encoder/)

Quick answer: Base64 converts any data, including images or Unicode text, into a string of 64 safe ASCII characters so it can travel through systems built for text. It is encoding, not encryption: anyone can decode it. BISCS India's Base64 tool encodes and decodes text or files, with URL-safe mode, entirely in your browser.

Base64 is a way of writing any data, whether text, an image or a PDF, using only 64 plain characters: `A–Z`, `a–z`, `0–9`, `+` and `/`. It exists because many systems, from email to JSON to HTML, were built to carry text and can corrupt raw binary bytes.

The most important thing to know is that Base64 is **encoding, not encryption**. It hides nothing. The [Base64 Encode / Decode](https://biscsindia.com/tools/base64-encoder/) tool on BISCS India converts both ways in your browser, handles Hindi, Bengali and emoji correctly, and can turn whole files into Base64 strings.

## How does Base64 work?

Computers store data as bytes of 8 bits. Base64 takes 3 bytes (24 bits) at a time, splits them into four 6-bit groups, and maps each group to one of 64 characters. When the input length is not a multiple of 3, the output is padded with one or two `=` signs.

The word `Hi!` is three bytes, so it becomes exactly four characters:

```text
Hi!      ->  SGkh
Hello    ->  SGVsbG8=
```

Because 3 bytes become 4 characters, Base64 output is always about one third larger than the input.

## Where you will meet Base64

- **Data URLs.** Small images embedded directly in CSS or HTML, such as `data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0…`.
- **Email attachments.** MIME email encodes attachments in Base64, wrapped at 76 characters per line.
- **JSON Web Tokens.** The header and payload of a JWT are base64url-encoded JSON.
- **HTTP Basic authentication.** The `Authorization: Basic …` header carries `username:password` in Base64, which is exactly why it must only be sent over HTTPS.
- **APIs that accept files.** Some government and business APIs, including several used for e-invoicing and document upload, expect file contents as a Base64 string inside JSON.

## Encoding is not encryption

This is the mistake that causes real security incidents. A developer stores an API key or password as Base64 in a config file or front-end code, thinking it is "encrypted". It is not. Decoding it is one click:

```js
atob('cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=');  // "password123"
```

Use Base64 to make data **transportable**, never to make it **secret**. For secrecy you need encryption with a key; for storing passwords you need a slow password hash such as bcrypt or Argon2.

## How to encode or decode with BISCS India

1. Open [Base64 Encode / Decode](https://biscsindia.com/tools/base64-encoder/).
2. Choose **Encode** or **Decode** at the top.
3. Type or paste your text into the left box. The result appears instantly on the right, with the byte size of each side.
4. Optional: tick **URL-safe (- _ no padding)** for base64url output, or **Wrap lines at 76 chars** for email-style formatting.
5. Use **Swap** to send the output back to the input and flip the mode, which is a quick way to check a round trip.
6. Click **Copy**, or **Download** to save the result. When decoding binary data, Download saves the original bytes.

### Encoding a file

Scroll to **File to Base64**, choose a file (up to 25 MB) and the Base64 appears in the output box. Keep **Include data: URL prefix** ticked if you want a ready-to-use `data:` URL, or untick it for the bare Base64 string that most APIs expect. For images specifically, the [Image to Base64](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-to-base64/) tool adds previews and ready-made HTML and CSS snippets.

## Unicode: why the Sample uses ₹ and नमस्ते

The browser’s built-in `btoa()` function throws an error on any character outside Latin-1, which rules out Hindi, Tamil, the rupee sign and emoji. The correct approach is to convert the text to UTF-8 bytes first:

```js
const bytes = new TextEncoder().encode('₹ नमस्ते');
const b64 = btoa(String.fromCharCode(...bytes));
```

The tool does this for you. When decoding, it checks that the bytes are valid UTF-8. If they are not, it shows a warning that the data is binary and offers a download instead of printing gibberish.

## Standard vs URL-safe Base64

| | Standard | URL-safe (base64url) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Characters 62 and 63 | `+` and `/` | `-` and `_` |
| Padding | `=` at the end | Usually omitted |
| Used in | Email, data URLs, most APIs | JWTs, URL parameters, file names |

The decoder accepts either variant, ignores whitespace and line breaks, and strips a leading `data:…;base64,` prefix automatically.

## How do I tell if a string is Base64?

There is no foolproof test, because many ordinary words are technically valid Base64. But a few signs are strong hints:

- The string uses only letters, digits, `+` and `/` (or `-` and `_` for the URL-safe form), with no spaces.
- Its length is a multiple of 4, often ending in one or two `=` signs.
- It starts with a familiar prefix. `iVBORw0KGgo` is the start of every PNG image, `/9j/` is a JPEG, `JVBERi0` is a PDF, and `eyJ` is how JSON beginning with `{"` followed by a letter usually encodes, which is why so many tokens start with those three letters.

The quickest check is to paste it into the decoder. If the result is readable text or JSON, you have your answer. If the tool reports binary data, use **Download** and open the file to see what it contains.

## Common mistakes with Base64

- **Treating it as security.** Covered above, but worth repeating.
- **Embedding big images as data URLs.** The 33% size increase and loss of browser caching usually make pages slower. Inline only tiny icons.
- **Double encoding.** Encoding an already-encoded string produces valid but useless output. If a decoded result still looks like Base64, it was encoded twice.
- **Mixing up Base64 and URL encoding.** A `+` in standard Base64 inside a URL may be read as a space. Use URL-safe Base64, or percent-encode the string with the [URL Encode / Decode](https://biscsindia.com/tools/url-encoder/) tool.
- **Breaking padding.** Removing or adding `=` characters by hand can make strict decoders reject the string.

## Privacy

Encoding happens in your browser with JavaScript. Text you type and files you select are never uploaded. That matters, because the strings people decode are often tokens and credentials. If you are inspecting a JWT, the [JWT Decoder](https://biscsindia.com/tools/jwt-decoder/) splits it into header and payload for you, again without sending it anywhere.

Q: Is Base64 a form of encryption?
A: No. Base64 is a reversible encoding with no key or secret. Anyone who sees a Base64 string can decode it in seconds. Never use it to hide passwords, API keys or personal data. If you need secrecy, use real encryption such as AES, and transport data over HTTPS.

Q: Why is Base64 output bigger than the original?
A: Base64 represents every 3 bytes of input as 4 characters, so output is about 33% larger, plus up to two = padding characters. A 300 KB image becomes roughly 400 KB of Base64 text. That overhead is why embedding large images as Base64 in web pages is usually a bad idea.

Q: What is URL-safe Base64?
A: Standard Base64 uses + and /, which have special meanings in URLs. URL-safe Base64, also called base64url, replaces them with - and _ and usually drops the = padding. JSON Web Tokens use this variant. The BISCS India decoder accepts both forms automatically.

Q: Why does decoding give me garbled text?
A: The original data was probably binary, such as an image, PDF or compressed file, rather than text. The tool detects this and warns you. Use Download to save the decoded bytes as a file, then rename it with the correct extension if you know what it is.

Q: Why does btoa() fail on Hindi or emoji text?
A: The browser function btoa only accepts characters in the Latin-1 range. To encode Unicode text you must first convert it to UTF-8 bytes, for example with TextEncoder, and then Base64-encode those bytes. The BISCS India tool does this automatically, so any language works.

## How to Split a Restaurant Bill and Tip Fairly Between Friends

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/how-to-split-a-bill-with-tip/
Tool: Tip & Bill Splitter (https://biscsindia.com/tools/bill-split-calculator/)

Quick answer: To split a bill, add the tip and any extra charges to the bill amount, then divide the total by the number of people. A ₹2,450 bill with a 10% tip is ₹2,695, or ₹673.75 each for four people. BISCS India’s free Tip & Bill Splitter does this instantly and can round shares for easy UPI payments.

To split a bill, add the tip and any extra charges to the bill, then divide by the number of people. For a ₹2,450 dinner with a 10% tip shared by four friends, the total is ₹2,695 and each person pays ₹673.75, or ₹674 if you round up to the nearest rupee.

That is simple on paper, but harder at a noisy table at the end of a long evening. The free [Tip & Bill Splitter](https://biscsindia.com/tools/bill-split-calculator/) works it out as you type and rounds each share to an amount that is easy to send by UPI.

## How do you split a bill with a tip?

The method has three steps:

1. **Tip** = bill × tip % ÷ 100.
2. **Total** = bill + tip + any tax or charge not already on the bill.
3. **Each share** = total ÷ number of people.

With the ₹2,450 example: tip = ₹245, total = ₹2,695, each share = ₹673.75.

Rounding matters in real life. If everyone pays ₹674, the group collects ₹2,696, which is ₹1 more than the total. Round up to the nearest ₹10 and everyone pays ₹680, collecting ₹2,720, so there is ₹25 extra. You can treat that as a slightly bigger tip.

3. Choose a **tip**: none, 5%, 10%, 15%, 20% or a custom percentage.
4. Add a **tax or service charge** percentage only if it is not already included in the bill.
5. Set the **number of people** with the plus and minus buttons, or type it.
6. Choose how to **round each share**: no rounding, or up to the nearest ₹1, ₹10, ₹50 or ₹100.
7. Read what each person pays, the grand total, the tip per person and any extra collected.

## Tipping and service charges in India

Tipping in India is customary in many sit-down restaurants but not compulsory. Many people leave around 5% to 10% for good service, though there is no fixed rule.

**Service charge is different from a tip.** Under guidelines from the Central Consumer Protection Authority issued in 2022, restaurants and hotels cannot add a service charge to the bill automatically or by default, and cannot refuse service if you decline it. If you see one, check the bill and ask for it to be removed if you do not wish to pay. If you do pay it, you probably do not need to tip again.

GST is normally printed on the bill already. Leave the tax field at zero in that case, or you will charge it twice.

## How to split unevenly but fairly

Even splits are easy, but they are not always fair. Someone may have skipped dessert, or ordered an expensive drink. A simple approach:

1. Subtract any **individual items** from the bill and note who had them.
2. Use the calculator to split the **shared amount** and tip equally.
3. Add each person's individual items to their share.

For a trip with many shared costs, such as a hotel, cabs and meals, it is often easiest to let one person pay and have everyone settle at the end with a single UPI transfer each.

## Splitting other shared expenses

The same approach works well beyond restaurants:

- **Flatmates' utilities.** Enter the electricity, internet or maid's salary as the bill, set the tip to none, and split by the number of flatmates.
- **Group gifts.** Collecting for a colleague's farewell or a friend's wedding gift is simply total ÷ number of contributors. Round up to ₹50 or ₹100 to keep transfers simple, and use any extra for a card or flowers.
- **Cab and auto rides.** Split the final fare, including tolls and parking, so nobody pays for the detour alone.
- **Trip bookings.** For a shared homestay or hotel, split the room charges equally, then handle meals and activities separately if spending differs.

The quick table of group sizes helps when you are not yet sure how many people will join. You can see at a glance what each person pays for 4, 5 or 6 people and share the right figure once everyone confirms.

## Common bill-splitting mistakes

- **Adding GST twice**, once from the bill and again in the tax field.
- **Tipping on top of a service charge** without noticing it is already there.
- **Rounding down**, which leaves the payer short.
- **Forgetting delivery or packing charges** on food orders.
- **Splitting by headcount when children ate little.** Agree how to handle it before the bill arrives.

## Tips for smooth group payments

- Decide the tip percentage before you start dividing, so no one debates it later.
- Round up to an amount that is easy to send, such as the nearest ₹10, and treat the extra as tip.
- Share a screenshot of the result in the group chat, so everyone sees the same number.
- If someone settles later, note it in the chat to avoid confusion.

Q: Do I have to pay a service charge at restaurants in India?
A: Guidelines issued by the Central Consumer Protection Authority in 2022 say restaurants cannot add a service charge automatically or by default, and cannot make it a condition of service. Tipping is voluntary. If a service charge appears on your bill and you do not wish to pay it, you can ask for it to be removed.

Q: Should the tip be calculated before or after GST?
A: Most people calculate the tip on the food and drink amount before tax, since GST goes to the government, not the staff. Either way is acceptable as long as the group agrees. In the calculator, enter the pre-tax amount as the bill and put the GST percentage in the tax field to tip on the pre-tax figure.

Q: What does the extra collected amount mean when rounding?
A: When each share is rounded up, say to the nearest ₹10, the group pays slightly more than the bill. The calculator shows this difference as extra collected. You can leave it as an additional tip or have the person who paid return it.

Q: Can the calculator split a bill unevenly?
A: It splits the total equally. For uneven bills, first subtract items that only one person had, split the shared amount equally with the tool, then add each person’s own items to their share. This keeps things fair without complicated maths.

## BMI Calculator Guide: Formula, Categories and Indian Cut-offs

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/bmi-calculator-indian-cut-offs-explained/
Tool: BMI Calculator (https://biscsindia.com/tools/bmi-calculator/)

Quick answer: BMI (Body Mass Index) is your weight in kilograms divided by your height in metres squared. Under WHO categories, 18.5–24.9 is a healthy range, but guidelines commonly used in India treat 23 and above as overweight for Asian Indian adults. BMI is a screening estimate only; BISCS India’s BMI Calculator shows both scales.

Body Mass Index (BMI) is your weight in kilograms divided by the square of your height in metres. A person who is 170 cm tall and weighs 68 kg has a BMI of 68 ÷ (1.70 × 1.70) = 23.5.

Whether 23.5 counts as "healthy" depends on which scale you use. Under the general WHO categories it is in the healthy range, but under the lower cut-offs commonly used for Asian Indian adults it falls just into "overweight". The free [BMI Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/bmi-calculator/) shows you either scale with one tick box.

**Important:** BMI is a quick screening estimate, not a diagnosis. It does not measure body fat directly, and it should not replace advice from a doctor or registered dietitian.

## What is the BMI formula?

The formula is the same everywhere:

**BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)²**

If you measure in feet and pounds, convert first, or let the calculator do it. For example, 5 feet 7 inches is 67 inches, or 1.70 m, and 150 lb is about 68.0 kg. That gives a BMI of about 23.5, the same as the metric example above.

## BMI categories: WHO and Asian Indian cut-offs

Research has found that people of South Asian origin tend to have more body fat, especially around the waist, and a higher risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease at a lower BMI than many other populations. For this reason, guidelines commonly cited in India use lower thresholds for adults.

| Category | WHO (general) | Asian / Indian cut-offs (commonly cited) |
|---|---|---|
| Underweight | Below 18.5 | Below 18.5 |
| Healthy weight | 18.5 – 24.9 | 18.5 – 22.9 |
| Overweight | 25 – 29.9 | 23 – 24.9 |
| Obese | 30 and above | 25 and above |

Different sources word these slightly differently. Some Indian guidance, for example, puts the lower end of normal at 18.0 rather than 18.5. The broad message is the same: for Indian adults, a BMI from 23 upwards deserves attention earlier than the WHO scale would suggest. Your doctor may also use other measures before drawing conclusions.

## How to check your BMI with the BISCS tool

1. Open the [BMI Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/bmi-calculator/).
2. Choose **Metric (cm, kg)** or **Imperial (ft, lb)**. Values carry over if you switch.
3. Enter your height and weight. Use a recent weight taken in light clothing.
4. Tick **Use Asian / Indian cut-offs** if you want the lower thresholds.
5. Read your BMI, category and position on the coloured scale.
6. Check the **healthy weight range** for your height, and the approximate change needed to reach it.

The tool also shows **BMI Prime**, which is your BMI divided by the upper limit of the healthy range for the scale you chose. A value below 1.0 means you are under that upper limit. Nothing you enter is uploaded, because the maths runs on your device.

## Worked example: the same person on two scales

Take Rahul, 170 cm and 68 kg, BMI 23.5.

- **WHO scale:** healthy. His healthy weight range is about 53.5 kg to 72.0 kg.
- **Asian cut-offs:** overweight, just above the 22.9 limit. His healthy range becomes about 53.5 kg to 66.2 kg, so the tool suggests losing about 1.8 kg to reach it.

Now take Priya, 160 cm and 82 kg. Her BMI is 82 ÷ 2.56 = 32.0, which is obese on both scales. The calculator shows a target that brings her into the healthy range, but a safe plan and pace should come from a doctor or dietitian, not from a number alone.

## What BMI cannot tell you

BMI is popular because it needs only a tape and a scale. Its limits are just as important:

- **It ignores body composition.** Muscle weighs more than fat for the same volume, so sportspeople and gym regulars can read as "overweight" while being fit.
- **It does not show where fat sits.** Fat around the abdomen carries more health risk than fat elsewhere.
- **It is for adults only.** Children and teenagers need age- and sex-specific growth charts.
- **It is not meant for pregnancy.** Weight gain during pregnancy follows different guidance.
- **It can miss risk in older adults,** who may lose muscle while keeping the same weight.

### Add a waist measurement

Many clinicians pair BMI with waist circumference. Thresholds commonly cited for Indian adults are around 90 cm for men and 80 cm for women, above which abdominal obesity is considered more likely. Measure midway between your lowest rib and the top of your hip bone, breathing out normally.

## Common mistakes when checking BMI

- Using height in centimetres without converting to metres (68 ÷ 170² gives a meaningless 0.0024).
- Weighing after a heavy meal or in shoes and outdoor clothes.
- Relying on an old height measurement. Adults can lose a little height with age.
- Reading a single result as a diagnosis rather than a reason to check further.
- Comparing your number with a friend's who uses a different scale.

## What to do with your result

If your BMI is in the healthy range, keep up regular activity and a balanced diet, and recheck every few months. If it is below or above the range:

- **Talk to a doctor** for a basic check-up. Blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol tests give far more insight than BMI alone.
- **See a registered dietitian** for a plan that fits your food habits, budget and any medical conditions.
- **Aim for gradual change.** Sudden crash diets are hard to sustain and can be unsafe.

To understand how much energy your body uses each day, try the [Calorie Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/calorie-calculator/), which estimates your BMR and maintenance calories. If your scale or tape uses unfamiliar units, the [Unit Converter](https://biscsindia.com/tools/unit-converter/) converts pounds, stones, feet and inches. And for an exact age to go with a health form, use the [Age Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/age-calculator/).

BMI is a useful first look, not the full story. Use the [BMI Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/bmi-calculator/) to know where you stand, then let a qualified professional help you decide what, if anything, to change.

Q: What is a healthy BMI for Indians?
A: Guidelines commonly cited in India suggest a BMI of roughly 18.5 to 22.9 as the healthy range for Asian Indian adults, with 23 to 24.9 classed as overweight and 25 or above as obese. These lower cut-offs reflect higher health risks at lower BMI seen in South Asian populations. A doctor can interpret your figure in context.

Q: Is BMI accurate for athletes and older adults?
A: Not always. BMI cannot tell muscle from fat, so muscular people can show a high BMI while being healthy, and older adults may have a normal BMI with low muscle and more body fat. Waist measurement, body composition and a medical check-up give a fuller picture.

Q: Can I use this BMI calculator for my child?
A: No. Adult BMI categories are meant for people aged 18 and over. Children and teenagers are assessed with BMI-for-age growth charts that compare them with others of the same age and sex. Ask a paediatrician to plot your child’s height and weight correctly.

Q: What should I do if my BMI is outside the healthy range?
A: Treat it as a prompt for a conversation, not a diagnosis. Book a check-up with a doctor, who may measure waist size, blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol. A registered dietitian can then suggest realistic changes to food and activity that suit your health and routine.

Q: Does the BMI calculator save my weight or height?
A: No. Everything is calculated in your browser as you type, and your measurements are not sent to or stored on any server. You can check figures for family members privately.

## CSS Box Shadow Generator: Soft, Layered and Inset Shadows

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/css-box-shadow-generator-guide/
Tool: Box Shadow Generator (https://biscsindia.com/tools/box-shadow-generator/)

Quick answer: The CSS box-shadow property draws a shadow around an element using up to five parts: horizontal offset, vertical offset, blur, spread and colour, plus an optional inset keyword. BISCS India's Box Shadow Generator lets you adjust each value with sliders, stack up to eight layers and copy the finished CSS, all in your browser.

The CSS `box-shadow` property adds depth to flat elements: a card that seems to float, a button that looks pressable, an input that appears recessed. One line of CSS replaces what used to need image files and extra markup.

The catch is that its five numbers interact in ways that are hard to picture. The [Box Shadow Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/box-shadow-generator/) on BISCS India solves that with sliders and a live preview. Adjust offset, blur, spread, colour and opacity, stack several layers, and copy the CSS once it looks right.

## The anatomy of a box-shadow

Here is a typical soft card shadow:

```css
box-shadow: 0px 10px 30px -5px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
```

Reading it left to right:

| Value | Name | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0px` | X offset | Moves the shadow right (positive) or left (negative) |
| `10px` | Y offset | Moves it down (positive) or up (negative) |
| `30px` | Blur | Softens the edge; 0 is a hard edge |
| `-5px` | Spread | Grows (positive) or shrinks (negative) the shadow |
| `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18)` | Colour | Usually black or a dark tint at low opacity |

Add the keyword `inset` at the start and the shadow is drawn inside the element instead, making it look pressed in.

## How to build a shadow with BISCS India

1. Open the [Box Shadow Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/box-shadow-generator/).
2. Click a preset to start: **Soft**, **Medium**, **Large**, **Hard**, **Glow**, **Layered**, **Neumorphic** or **Inset**.
3. Fine-tune with the sliders or number fields: **X offset** and **Y offset** (−100 to 100 px), **Blur** (0 to 200 px), **Spread** (−100 to 100 px) and **Opacity** (0 to 1).
4. Pick a shadow **Colour** and tick **Inset** if you want an inner shadow.
5. Match the preview to your design by setting the **Corner radius**, **Box colour** and **Background**. A shadow that looks good on white can look heavy on a grey page.
6. Click **Add layer** to stack another shadow (up to eight). Select a layer chip to edit it, or **Remove layer** to delete it.
7. Click **Copy CSS**.

## Why negative spread makes shadows look natural

Beginners often crank up the blur and wonder why the shadow looks like a grey cloud around the whole card. In real life, an object lifted off a surface casts a shadow mostly beneath it, not around its sides.

A negative spread shrinks the shadow before it is blurred, so it hides behind the element at the sides and peeks out mainly at the bottom, thanks to the positive Y offset. Compare:

```css
/* Muddy halo */
box-shadow: 0 0 30px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.3);

/* Lifted card */
box-shadow: 0 10px 30px -5px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
```

## Layered shadows for realistic depth

Real shadows have a sharp, dark core close to the object and a wide, faint area further away. A single CSS shadow cannot do both, but several stacked shadows can. The **Layered** preset uses five shadows that double in size each time:

```css
box-shadow:
  0 1px 1px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.08),
  0 2px 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.08),
  0 4px 4px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.08),
  0 8px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.08),
  0 16px 16px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.08);
```

Each layer is very light on its own; together they produce a smooth, believable falloff. This approach is popular in modern design systems because it looks good on any background.

## Shadow styles and when to use them

- **Soft:** cards, modals and dropdown menus on light backgrounds.
- **Medium:** small UI elements like buttons and chips that need a gentle lift.
- **Large:** pop-ups and dialogs that should feel clearly above the page.
- **Hard:** zero blur and an offset, giving a flat, retro or "neo-brutalist" look.
- **Glow:** a coloured shadow with no offset, useful for focus states or highlighting a primary call to action.
- **Neumorphic:** a light shadow on one side and a dark one on the other, so the element seems extruded from the background. It only works when the element and background are the same colour, and it often has poor contrast, so use it sparingly.
- **Inset:** input fields, toggles and pressed button states.

## Design tips

- **Keep one light source.** If shadows on your page point down, all of them should. Mixed directions look odd.
- **Use elevation levels.** Define three or four shadows, for example resting, raised, floating and modal, and reuse them across the site instead of inventing new ones.
- **Tint shadows on coloured backgrounds.** On a blue background, a dark blue shadow looks richer than pure black.
- **Respect dark mode.** Shadows are barely visible on dark backgrounds. Many dark themes use lighter surface colours or subtle borders to show depth instead.
- **Do not rely on shadows alone.** An outline or slight background difference helps people with low vision tell where a card begins.

## Common mistakes

- **Opacity too high.** A shadow at 0.5 or more looks heavy and dated. Most interface shadows sit between 0.05 and 0.25.
- **Forgetting `border-radius`.** The shadow follows the element’s corners. If the card is rounded but the shadow preview was square, the result will not match. Set the same radius in the generator.
- **Shadows cut off.** A parent with `overflow: hidden` clips child shadows. Add padding to the parent or move the overflow rule.
- **Animating `box-shadow` directly.** It can be janky on slower phones. Animate the opacity of a pseudo-element that carries the shadow instead.
- **Using shadows as borders.** `0 0 0 1px` is a neat trick for a border that does not affect layout, but a real `border` or `outline` is clearer for accessibility tools.

## Pair it with other CSS tools

Shadows look best with a thoughtful background. Try a subtle gradient from the [CSS Gradient Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/css-gradient-generator/) behind a white card, and choose a shadow tint that matches your palette using the [Color Converter](https://biscsindia.com/tools/color-converter/).

## Privacy

The preview is rendered by your browser and the CSS is generated on the page. Nothing is uploaded or saved, and there is no sign-up or watermark.

Q: What is the order of values in box-shadow?
A: The order is horizontal offset, vertical offset, blur radius, spread radius and colour, for example 0 10px 30px -5px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18). Offsets are required; blur and spread are optional and default to zero. The inset keyword can go at the start or the end, and multiple shadows are separated by commas.

Q: What is the difference between blur and spread?
A: Blur controls how soft the shadow’s edge is: zero gives a hard edge, larger values fade it out over more pixels. Spread grows or shrinks the shadow before blurring. A positive spread makes it bigger than the element, and a negative spread pulls it inwards, which is the secret to soft, natural shadows.

Q: Does box-shadow slow down a website?
A: Static shadows are cheap for modern browsers. Problems arise mainly when very large, heavily blurred shadows are animated, or when hundreds of shadowed elements scroll on low-end phones. To animate a shadow smoothly, fade in a pseudo-element that already has the shadow, rather than animating box-shadow itself.

Q: Why use rgba instead of a solid colour for shadows?
A: Real shadows are partly transparent, letting the background show through. A solid grey shadow looks flat and wrong on coloured backgrounds. A black or dark-tinted colour at low opacity, typically 0.05 to 0.25, blends naturally with whatever is behind the element.

Q: What is the difference between box-shadow and drop-shadow?
A: box-shadow follows the element’s rectangular box, including rounded corners. The CSS filter drop-shadow follows the actual visible shape, including transparent areas of a PNG or SVG. Use box-shadow for cards and buttons, and drop-shadow for irregular shapes like icons or cut-out product photos.

## CAGR Calculator: Compound Annual Growth Rate Made Simple

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/cagr-formula-calculator-explained/
Tool: CAGR Calculator (https://biscsindia.com/tools/cagr-calculator/)

Quick answer: CAGR is the steady yearly growth rate that turns a starting value into an ending value: CAGR = (final ÷ initial)^(1 ÷ years) − 1. An investment that grows from ₹1 lakh to ₹2.5 lakh in 5 years has a CAGR of about 20.11%. BISCS India's free CAGR Calculator finds the rate or projects a future value from one.

CAGR, or compound annual growth rate, is the constant yearly rate at which a value would have to grow to get from its starting point to its ending point over a given number of years. The formula is **CAGR = (final value ÷ initial value)^(1 ÷ years) − 1**.

If your mutual fund investment of ₹1,00,000 is worth ₹2,50,000 after 5 years, the CAGR is (2.5)^(1/5) − 1, about **20.11% a year**. The free [CAGR Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/cagr-calculator/) on BISCS India does this sum and can also work the other way, projecting a future value from a growth rate.

## Why use CAGR instead of total return?

Total (absolute) return tells you how much something grew in all, but not how fast. A 150% gain sounds impressive, but it means something very different over 5 years than over 15. CAGR puts every investment or business metric on the same yearly scale so you can compare them fairly.

It also smooths out the bumps. Real investments rarely grow at the same rate every year. CAGR answers a simpler question: "What steady yearly rate would have produced this result?"

## How to use the BISCS CAGR Calculator

1. Open the [CAGR Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/cagr-calculator/).
2. Choose what you want to find: **CAGR** or **Future value**.
3. For CAGR, enter the **initial value**, the **final value** and the **duration** in years. Fractions like 3.5 are fine.
4. For future value, enter the **initial value**, a **CAGR** and the **duration**.
5. Read the result: the growth rate with absolute return and growth multiple, or the projected value and total gain.
6. Look at the year-by-year table to see the value path at that steady rate.

The formula used is printed on the result, and nothing you type leaves your browser.

## Worked examples

| What is measured | Start | End | Years | CAGR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mutual fund lump sum | ₹1,00,000 | ₹2,50,000 | 5 | 20.11% |
| Shop's annual revenue | ₹40 lakh | ₹65 lakh | 4 | 12.91% |
| Flat bought and sold | ₹45 lakh | ₹72 lakh | 9 | 5.36% |
| A share price | ₹500 | ₹800 | 3 | 16.96% |

The flat example is a useful reality check. A ₹27 lakh gain feels large, but spread over nine years it is about 5.36% a year, before stamp duty, registration, maintenance, brokerage and capital gains tax. Comparing that rate with what a deposit or fund earned over the same period puts the result in perspective.

Projecting forward works too: ₹1 lakh growing at a CAGR of 15% for 7 years reaches about ₹2,66,002.

## Using CAGR to set business targets

CAGR also works in reverse for planning. If a Surat textile trader wants to double annual sales in five years, the growth needed is 2^(1/5) − 1, about **14.87% a year**. Tripling sales over ten years needs about **11.61% a year**. These figures are often more useful than a vague "double the business" goal, because you can compare them with what the business has actually managed so far.

To check a target in the calculator, choose **Future value**, enter this year's sales as the initial value, type the CAGR you think is realistic and set the years. The year-by-year table then gives a milestone for each year, which you can track against your actual sales. If last year's revenue growth was 8%, a 15% target is a big stretch, and the gap tells you how much needs to change.

| Goal | Years | CAGR needed |
|---|---|---|
| Double | 5 | 14.87% |
| Double | 10 | 7.18% |
| Triple | 10 | 11.61% |

## CAGR vs average return: why it matters

Imagine an investment of ₹1 lakh that gains 50% in year one (₹1.5 lakh) and loses 50% in year two (₹75,000). The simple average of +50% and −50% is 0%, which suggests you broke even. In fact you lost ₹25,000. The CAGR is about −13.4% a year, which matches your real experience.

This is why fund factsheets and company reports quote CAGR rather than averages for multi-year performance.

## When CAGR is the right tool, and when it is not

**Good uses:**
- Comparing lump-sum investments held for different periods.
- Measuring growth in sales, profit, users or prices between two dates.
- Checking the real annual growth of a property, gold or a share you bought and sold.
- Setting a realistic return assumption for the [Lumpsum Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/lumpsum-calculator/).

**Poor uses:**
- SIPs or any investment with several deposits or withdrawals; use XIRR instead. The [SIP Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/sip-calculator/) projects SIPs from an assumed return.
- Judging risk. Two investments can have the same CAGR but very different ups and downs along the way.
- Very short periods, where a single good or bad month can distort the yearly rate.

## Common mistakes

1. **Dividing total return by the number of years.** 150% ÷ 5 = 30% is not the CAGR; the correct figure is about 20.11%.
2. **Getting the years wrong.** Count the actual time held. Three years and six months is 3.5, not 3 or 4.
3. **Ignoring costs and taxes.** CAGR on prices excludes brokerage, stamp duty, fees and tax unless you include them in the values.
4. **Ignoring inflation.** A 6% CAGR when prices rose 6% a year is roughly no real growth. Check with the [Inflation Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/inflation-calculator/).
5. **Assuming past CAGR will continue.** It describes history, not the future.

## Limits and a reminder

CAGR is a single summary number. It hides volatility, the timing of gains and the order of returns, and it says nothing about the risks you took. The calculator handles values of zero or more for the final amount and any positive duration, but negative starting values are outside what the formula can describe.

This article is general information for understanding growth rates, not investment advice. Before acting on past performance figures, check official fund documents on AMFI or your fund house's site, and consider guidance from a SEBI-registered adviser.

Q: What is the difference between CAGR and absolute return?
A: Absolute return is the total percentage gain over the whole period, ignoring time. CAGR spreads that gain into an equivalent yearly rate. Growing from ₹1 lakh to ₹2.5 lakh is a 150% absolute return, but over five years that is a CAGR of about 20.11% a year.

Q: Is CAGR the same as average annual return?
A: No. The simple average of yearly returns can be misleading. If an investment rises 50% one year and falls 50% the next, the average is 0%, but you have actually lost 25% of your money. The CAGR over those two years is about −13.4%, which reflects what really happened.

Q: Can I use CAGR for SIP investments?
A: Not accurately. CAGR assumes a single starting amount and a single ending amount. A SIP has many investments on different dates, so its return is usually measured with XIRR, which accounts for each cash flow. Use CAGR for lump sums, prices, NAVs, revenue or other start-and-end values.

Q: Can I enter a period that is not a whole number of years?
A: Yes. Duration can be fractional, such as 5.5 years for five years and six months. A shorter or longer period changes the result noticeably: ₹1 lakh growing to ₹2.5 lakh in 5.5 years is a CAGR of about 18.13%, compared with 20.11% over exactly 5 years.

## How Many Calories Do I Need a Day? BMR and TDEE Explained

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/how-many-calories-do-i-need-bmr-tdee/
Tool: Calorie Calculator (https://biscsindia.com/tools/calorie-calculator/)

Quick answer: Your daily calorie need is roughly your BMR (energy used at rest) multiplied by an activity factor, giving your TDEE or maintenance calories. BISCS India’s Calorie Calculator uses the Mifflin–St Jeor equation to estimate both, plus targets for gradual weight loss or gain. Treat the result as an estimate and consult a doctor or dietitian.

The number of calories you need each day depends on your body size, age, sex and how active you are. A common way to estimate it is to work out your **BMR** (the energy your body uses at rest) and multiply it by an **activity factor** to get your **TDEE** (total daily energy expenditure). Eating close to your TDEE keeps your weight roughly stable.

For a 30-year-old man who is 170 cm tall, weighs 70 kg and exercises lightly, that comes to about 2,224 kcal a day. The free [Calorie Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/calorie-calculator/) works this out for you in seconds.

**Please note:** these are estimates for healthy adults. They are not medical advice. If you have a health condition, are pregnant, or plan a significant change in diet, consult a doctor or registered dietitian.

## What are BMR and TDEE?

- **BMR (basal metabolic rate)** is the energy needed to keep you alive at complete rest: breathing, heartbeat, temperature and organ function. For most people it makes up the largest share of daily energy use.
- **TDEE (total daily energy expenditure)** is BMR plus everything else: walking, working, household chores, exercise and digesting food.

Your TDEE is your **maintenance calories**. Eat less than this on average and you tend to lose weight; eat more and you tend to gain.

## The formula behind the calculator

The BISCS tool uses the **Mifflin–St Jeor equation**, which is widely used by dietitians as a starting estimate:

- **Men:** BMR = 10 × weight (kg) + 6.25 × height (cm) − 5 × age + 5
- **Women:** BMR = 10 × weight (kg) + 6.25 × height (cm) − 5 × age − 161

BMR is then multiplied by an activity factor:

| Activity level | Description | Multiplier |
|---|---|---|
| Sedentary | Little or no exercise | 1.2 |
| Light | Exercise 1–3 days a week | 1.375 |
| Moderate | Exercise 3–5 days a week | 1.55 |
| Active | Hard exercise 6–7 days a week | 1.725 |
| Very active | Physical job or training twice a day | 1.9 |

## How to use the BISCS Calorie Calculator

1. Open the [Calorie Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/calorie-calculator/).
2. Choose your **sex** and **units** (metric or imperial).
3. Enter your **age** (15 to 100), **height** and **weight**.
4. Pick the **activity level** that matches a typical week.
5. Read your maintenance calories at the top, with your BMR shown beside it.
6. Check the **goal table** for calorie targets to lose, maintain or gain weight, and the suggested macro split.

The calculation happens in your browser, so your age and weight are not uploaded anywhere.

## Worked examples

### Arjun: light activity, wants to lose weight slowly

Arjun is 30, 170 cm and 70 kg, and goes to the gym twice a week.

- BMR = 700 + 1,062.5 − 150 + 5 = 1,617.5, shown as about 1,618 kcal.
- TDEE = 1,617.5 × 1.375 ≈ 2,224 kcal.
- A 500 kcal daily deficit gives a target of about 1,724 kcal.

At maintenance, the suggested split of 25% protein, 50% carbohydrate and 25% fat works out to about 139 g protein, 278 g carbohydrate and 62 g fat. These are starting points; a dietitian may adjust them for his goals.

### Meena: sedentary desk job

Meena is 28, 158 cm and 60 kg, and rarely exercises.

- BMR = 600 + 987.5 − 140 − 161 = 1,286.5, about 1,287 kcal.
- TDEE = 1,286.5 × 1.2 ≈ 1,544 kcal.
- A 500 kcal deficit would mean about 1,044 kcal a day.

The calculator marks that last figure as **low**, because it is below roughly 1,200 kcal. For Meena, a milder 250 kcal deficit (about 1,294 kcal) combined with more daily movement is a more sustainable option, and worth discussing with a professional.

## How fast can you safely lose or gain weight?

The goal table uses rough rules of thumb: a deficit of about 500 kcal a day is often linked to around 0.5 kg of loss per week, and 250 kcal to around 0.25 kg. Real results vary because water, muscle, hormones and how accurately you track food all play a part.

Gradual change is usually easier to sustain. Very low intakes can make it hard to get enough protein and micronutrients, and the tool deliberately flags targets below about 1,200 kcal for women and 1,500 kcal for men. Going under those levels should only happen with medical supervision.

## Common mistakes with calorie targets

- **Overstating activity.** Choosing "Active" because of one intense week inflates the number.
- **Treating the result as exact.** Formulas estimate averages; your real need may be a few hundred calories different.
- **Forgetting cooking oil, ghee and drinks.** Tea with sugar, juices and the oil in a tadka add up quickly.
- **Changing everything at once.** Adjust intake by small steps and watch the trend for two to four weeks.
- **Ignoring protein.** A low-calorie diet that is also low in protein can cost muscle.
- **Using it for children, teenagers or pregnancy.** These need professional guidance.

## Practical tips

- Weigh yourself at the same time of day, a few times a week, and look at the weekly average.
- Read nutrition labels on packaged foods; they list energy per serving and per 100 g.
- Recalculate after a change of 3 to 5 kg, since your needs change with your weight.
- Combine diet changes with activity. Even a daily brisk walk raises your TDEE.

For a quick health snapshot alongside this, the [BMI Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/bmi-calculator/) shows your BMI on both WHO and Asian Indian scales. If your recipes use cups, ounces or pounds, the [Unit Converter](https://biscsindia.com/tools/unit-converter/) handles kitchen units. And to time workouts or intervals, try the [Stopwatch & Timer](https://biscsindia.com/tools/stopwatch-timer/).

Calorie numbers are a helpful guide, not a rulebook. Use the [Calorie Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/calorie-calculator/) to get a sensible starting point, then let your progress, and a qualified dietitian or doctor, shape the details.

Q: What is the difference between BMR and TDEE?
A: BMR, or basal metabolic rate, is the energy your body uses at complete rest to keep you alive: breathing, circulation and organ function. TDEE, or total daily energy expenditure, adds the energy used in daily movement and exercise. TDEE is the figure to use as your maintenance calories.

Q: How accurate is a calorie calculator?
A: It gives a reasonable starting estimate, not an exact measurement. Formulas such as Mifflin–St Jeor are based on population averages, so an individual’s real needs can differ noticeably. Track your weight for a few weeks at a given intake and adjust gradually, ideally with guidance from a dietitian.

Q: Is it safe to eat 1,000 calories a day to lose weight fast?
A: Very low intakes are generally not advisable without medical supervision. They can make it hard to get enough protein, vitamins and minerals, and are difficult to sustain. The calculator flags targets below about 1,200 kcal for women and 1,500 kcal for men. Speak to a doctor before trying any aggressive diet.

Q: Which activity level should I choose?
A: Pick the level that matches your typical week, not your best week. Most people with desk jobs and a few workouts fit “Light” or “Moderate”. If you are unsure, choose the lower option, then adjust after watching your weight trend for two to four weeks.

Q: Can I use this calculator during pregnancy or for a child?
A: No. The formula is designed for healthy adults and does not account for pregnancy, breastfeeding, growth in children and teenagers, or medical conditions that affect metabolism. In those situations, calorie needs should come from a doctor or registered dietitian.

## Title Case vs Sentence case: which should you use?

Both are correct, and style guides disagree, so the main rule is to pick one and be consistent.

**Title Case** gives headings a formal, traditional look. The BISCS converter follows the common convention of leaving short words such as "a", "an", "the", "and", "of", "in", "to" and "with" in lower case, unless they are the first or last word or come straight after a colon. So "a guide to gst for small shops" becomes "A Guide to Gst for Small Shops".

**Sentence case** reads more naturally and is easier to scan, which is why many government portals, apps and news sites use it for headings and buttons. The converter capitalises the first letter after each full stop, question mark, exclamation mark or Hindi purna viram, and fixes a lone "i" to "I".

Look at that Title Case example again: "Gst" is wrong. That leads to the most important tip.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- **Losing acronyms and proper nouns.** No converter can tell that GST, PAN, UPI, Kolkata or your company name should stay as they are. Always proofread after converting and fix them by hand.
- **Using UPPER CASE for long text.** Paragraphs in capitals are harder to read and come across as shouting in emails and WhatsApp messages. Keep capitals for short labels.
- **Converting code that is already mixed.** The programming styles split words at spaces, punctuation and changes from lower to upper case, so `HTTPServerError` becomes `http_server_error`. Check edge cases like version numbers.
- **Expecting Indian scripts to change.** Hindi, Bengali, Tamil and most Indian scripts have no capital letters, so they are left untouched.

## Tips for developers and data work

The programming styles treat each line separately. That makes the tool handy for bulk renaming:

- Paste the header row of a spreadsheet, one column name per line, and convert to `snake_case` before importing into a database.
- Turn a list of labels like "First Name", "Date of Birth" and "PAN Number" into `camelCase` JSON keys: `firstName`, `dateOfBirth`, `panNumber`.
- Convert component names to `kebab-case` for file names and CSS classes.

If you are building URLs from page titles, the dedicated [Slug Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/slug-generator/) is a better fit because it also strips punctuation, handles accents and can drop stop words. When you need to rename one term throughout a long file rather than change case, use [Find and Replace](https://biscsindia.com/tools/find-and-replace/).

Data entered by many different people is rarely consistent. A customer list may contain "RAMESH KUMAR", "priya sharma" and "Anil  verma" in the same column. A quick clean-up routine looks like this:

No. The conversion happens with JavaScript in your browser, so nothing is sent to BISCS India's servers. The undo history lasts only while the page is open, up to 50 steps, and disappears when you close the tab or clear the box.

That makes it suitable for working on client lists, unpublished articles or internal documents, though as always it is wise to use your own device for anything sensitive.

Q: What is the difference between Title Case and Sentence case?
A: Title Case capitalises the main words of a heading, as in How to File Your Income Tax Return, while leaving short words like of, and, to in lower case. Sentence case capitalises only the first word and proper nouns, as in How to file your income tax return. News sites and government pages increasingly prefer sentence case.

A: Not automatically. A tool cannot know which words are proper nouns or acronyms, so Sentence case and lower case will turn GST into gst and Delhi into delhi. After converting, scan the result and fix names, brands and abbreviations by hand. The undo button lets you step back if needed.

## How to Minify CSS, HTML and JSON Online (and What It Saves)

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/minify-css-html-json-online/
Tool: CSS / HTML / JSON Minifier (https://biscsindia.com/tools/code-minifier/)

Quick answer: Minifying code removes whitespace, line breaks and comments that browsers do not need, making CSS, HTML and JSON files smaller and slightly faster to download. BISCS India's CSS / HTML / JSON Minifier does this in your browser, keeps licence comments and preformatted content intact, and shows exactly how many bytes you saved.

Minifying code means stripping out everything a browser does not need: indentation, line breaks, comments and redundant characters. The page looks and works exactly the same, but the file is smaller, so it downloads and parses a little faster.

The [CSS / HTML / JSON Minifier](https://biscsindia.com/tools/code-minifier/) on BISCS India handles all three formats in one place. Paste your code or upload a file, and it shows the minified output alongside the original size, the new size and the percentage saved.

## What does minification remove?

Take this small piece of CSS:

```css
/* Card component */
.card {
  display: flex;
  padding: 16px 20px;
  color: #333333;
}
```

Minified, it becomes:

```css
.card{display:flex;padding:16px 20px;color:#333333}
```

The comment, newlines and indentation are gone, spaces around `{`, `:` and `;` are removed, and the final semicolon before `}` is dropped because CSS does not require it. Every remaining character is needed.

For HTML, the minifier collapses runs of whitespace between tags and removes ordinary comments. For JSON, it removes all whitespace between tokens.

## How to minify code with BISCS India

1. Open the [CSS / HTML / JSON Minifier](https://biscsindia.com/tools/code-minifier/).
2. Choose the language at the top: **CSS**, **HTML** or **JSON**.
3. Paste your code, drop a file onto the input, or click **Upload** to load a `.css`, `.html`, `.htm` or `.json` file. **Sample** loads an example if you want to see it work first.
4. For CSS, decide whether to tick **Keep /*! licence */ comments**. It is on by default.
5. The minified output appears immediately, with **Original**, **Minified** and **Saved** figures underneath.
6. Copy the result or download it, and use it as your production file.

When you upload a file, the tool picks the matching language from its extension, so a `.json` file switches to JSON mode automatically. The download button names the output sensibly too, for example `styles.min.css`, which keeps it clearly separate from your editable source.

If you paste invalid JSON in JSON mode, the tool reports the error with its line and column instead of producing output.

## What the HTML minifier is careful to keep

Whitespace in HTML is not always meaningless, so the minifier leaves certain things alone:

- **Content of `pre` and `textarea` elements**, where spaces and line breaks are visible to users.
- **Inline `script` and `style` blocks**, which are passed through unchanged rather than risk breaking code.
- **Conditional comments** used for old Internet Explorer, in case your template still includes them.
- **A single space between inline elements**, because removing it would glue words together, for example between a bold word and the next one.

Ordinary comments such as `<!-- page styles -->` are removed. If you have template comments that a CMS or framework needs, check the output before publishing.

## Minification vs compression: what is the difference?

| | Minification | Gzip or Brotli compression |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where it happens | Once, before you upload the file | On the server for every response (or pre-compressed) |
| What it does | Removes unnecessary characters | Encodes repeated patterns more efficiently |
| Output | Still valid, readable-by-browser code | Binary, decoded by the browser automatically |
| Removes comments | Yes | No |
| Typical setup | Build tool or a minifier like this one | Hosting or CDN setting |

They work best together. Most hosting platforms, including popular static hosts and CDNs, apply compression automatically; minification is the part you control.

## How much will I actually save?

It depends on how the code was written. Heavily commented, well-indented CSS can shrink by a third or more. Already-compact code saves little. The **Saved** figure tells you the real number for your file, so there is no need to guess.

Keep perspective, though. A 6 KB stylesheet becoming 4 KB is a nice tidy-up, but if your page also loads a 2 MB hero photo, compressing that image will matter far more. The [Compress Image](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-compressor/) tool is a better first stop for slow pages.

## When should you minify?

- **Small websites without a build step.** A hand-written landing page or portfolio site can be minified manually before upload.
- **Email templates.** Some email clients have size limits that clip long messages, so trimming HTML weight can help keep the whole email visible.
- **Embedding JSON in configuration.** Environment variables and some API fields need JSON on a single line.
- **Quick checks.** Even if your build pipeline minifies automatically, it is useful to see how much a stylesheet shrinks.

If your project uses a framework or bundler such as Vite, Next.js or webpack, minification is usually already built into the production build. Use this tool for one-off files and for everything outside that pipeline.

## A simple workflow for small sites

If you maintain a small business website by hand, a light routine keeps things tidy without a build system. Keep a `src` folder with your readable `style.css` and HTML pages. When you are ready to publish, minify each changed file, save the output into a separate `public` folder, upload that folder, and open the live site on your phone to check nothing broke. Next time you need a change, edit the files in `src` and repeat. It takes a minute and keeps your editable code and your published code from ever getting mixed up.

## Common mistakes

- **Editing the minified file.** Always edit the readable source and minify again. Keep the minified file as an output, with a name like `style.min.css`.
- **Deleting licence notices.** Many open-source licences require the copyright comment to stay. Keep the `/*!` option on for third-party CSS.
- **Minifying broken code.** Errors become harder to spot on one long line. Validate first; for JSON, the [JSON Formatter](https://biscsindia.com/tools/json-formatter/) points to the exact error.
- **Forgetting to test.** After replacing a stylesheet or template with its minified version, load the page once on desktop and mobile.
- **Expecting JavaScript support.** Inline scripts are left untouched, and separate `.js` files need a dedicated JavaScript minifier.

## Readability first, size second

Write code for people, with clear indentation and helpful comments, and let tools make it small for machines. If you ever need to escape snippets of HTML for documentation rather than shrink them, the [HTML Entity Encoder](https://biscsindia.com/tools/html-entity-encoder/) is the right tool.

## Privacy

Your code is processed entirely in the browser. Nothing is uploaded, which means unreleased designs, client templates and internal configuration files stay on your computer.

Q: Does minifying CSS or HTML change how the page looks?
A: It should not. Minification only removes characters that have no effect on rendering, such as indentation, comments and redundant semicolons. Whitespace that matters, for example inside pre and textarea elements, is preserved. Always test the minified page once, because unusual markup or CSS hacks can occasionally behave differently.

Q: Is minification still worth it if my server uses gzip or Brotli?
A: Usually yes, but the gain is smaller. Compression already shrinks repeated whitespace very efficiently, so a file that is 30% smaller after minifying might be only a few percent smaller after compression. Minifying also removes comments, which can contain internal notes you would rather not publish.

Q: Can I minify JavaScript with this tool?
A: No. This tool handles CSS, HTML and JSON. Safely minifying JavaScript requires understanding variable scope and syntax in depth, which is the job of dedicated tools such as Terser or esbuild, usually run as part of a build process. Inline script blocks inside HTML are left unchanged.

Q: Can I un-minify code later?
A: You can re-format minified code so it is readable again, but comments and original formatting that were removed are gone for good. Always keep your original, readable source files and treat the minified version as a build output, never as the file you edit.

Q: What does Keep /*! licence */ comments mean?
A: By convention, a comment whose opening marker is followed by an exclamation mark holds a licence or copyright notice that should survive minification. Many open-source licences require that notice to stay with the code. With the option ticked, the minifier removes ordinary comments but keeps these special ones.

## Flip a Coin or Roll Dice Online: Fair Tosses and Real Odds

## The real odds behind coins and dice

### Coins

- Heads or tails: **1 in 2 (50%)** on every toss.
- Two heads in a row: 1 in 4 (25%).
- Five heads in a row: **1 in 32 (about 3.1%)**.

That last figure surprises people. In a long session of tossing, runs of five or more are common. They do not mean the coin is broken.

### One die

Each face has a **1 in 6** chance, about 16.7%. The average roll over time is **3.5**.

In Ludo, you often need a 6 to move a piece out. The chance of getting at least one 6 in three rolls is about **42%**, and in four rolls about **52%**. So waiting several turns for a 6 is completely normal.

### Two dice

With two dice there are 36 equally likely combinations, but the totals are not equally likely:

| Total | Ways to make it | Chance |
|---|---|---|
| 2 or 12 | 1 | About 2.8% each |
| 3 or 11 | 2 | About 5.6% each |
| 4 or 10 | 3 | About 8.3% each |
| 5 or 9 | 4 | About 11.1% each |
| 6 or 8 | 5 | About 13.9% each |
| 7 | 6 | About 16.7% |

The average total with two dice is **7**. Roll a few dozen times and watch the history's average total drift towards it.

## How the tool keeps it fair

Every flip and die face is chosen with the browser's `crypto.getRandomValues`, using a method that avoids the small bias some simple random generators introduce. The animation is decoration only; the result is decided first and the coin or dice are then turned to show it. That means fancy-looking spins cannot be "nudged" by timing your taps.

## Is a virtual toss as good as a real one?

For deciding things fairly, yes. A real coin's outcome depends on how hard it is flicked, how it is caught and the surface it lands on, which is why people sometimes argue about a "bad toss". A physical die can be slightly uneven, especially cheap ones with scooped-out dots. A secure random generator has none of these quirks.

What a virtual toss lacks is the ceremony and the feeling that everyone saw it. If that matters, put the screen where everyone can see it before pressing the button, and agree on the call first. In a formal match or competition, follow whatever method the organisers or rules require.

## A quick classroom experiment

Probability makes more sense when you see it happen:

1. Ask the class to predict how many heads they will get in 10 flips, then in 100.
2. Flip 10 times and note the result. It may well be 3 or 7 heads.
3. Keep going to 100 flips. The percentage will usually move much closer to 50%.
4. Discuss why small samples swing widely and large samples settle, which is the law of large numbers.
5. Switch to two dice and test whether 7 really appears most often.

## Common misunderstandings

- **"Tails is due."** Past tosses never change the next one.
- **"The app is rigged because I got 7 heads out of 10."** That happens about 12% of the time with a fair coin.
- **"All dice totals are equally likely."** With two or more dice, middle totals are far more common.
- **"Animations decide the outcome."** The result is chosen randomly; the animation just shows it.

## Tips for using it

- Agree on what heads and tails mean **before** flipping, so nobody argues afterwards.
- For a best-of-three decision, keep the tally visible on screen.
- For dice with more sides, such as a d20, use the [Random Number Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/random-number-generator/) with a range of 1 to 20.
- To pick a person rather than a side, the [Random Name Picker](https://biscsindia.com/tools/random-picker/) chooses from a list, and can split the group into teams.

Whether it is a cricket toss on the street or a Ludo game with missing dice, the [Coin Flip & Dice Roller](https://biscsindia.com/tools/coin-dice-roller/) gives you a fair result in a second.

Q: Is an online coin toss really 50/50?
A: Yes. The BISCS tool picks heads or tails using your browser’s cryptographically secure random generator, with exactly equal chances. Real coins are very close to 50/50 too, though studies suggest tiny biases from how they are flipped. Over a small number of tosses, uneven tallies are normal and do not indicate unfairness.

Q: After five heads in a row, is tails more likely?
A: No. Each toss is independent, so the next one is still exactly 50/50. Believing a result is overdue is called the gambler’s fallacy. A streak of five heads has a 1 in 32 chance from any given starting point, so streaks like this happen regularly over a long session.

Q: What is the most common total with two dice?
A: Seven. There are six ways to make it out of 36 possible combinations, so it comes up about one time in six. Totals of 2 and 12 are the rarest, with only one combination each, about one time in 36.

Q: Can I roll more than two dice?
A: Yes. Choose from 1 to 10 standard six-sided dice. The tool shows each die, the total, and a history table of every roll along with the average and highest total. For dice with other numbers of sides, use the Random Number Generator with the range you need.

## HEX to RGB and HSL Colour Converter (With Contrast Check)

BISCS India's Color Converter handles HEX, RGB, HSL, HSV and CMYK, shows tints and shades, and checks WCAG text contrast, all inside your browser.

A colour converter translates one colour into every other format you might need. Type `#FF9933`, the saffron of the Indian flag, and you instantly get `rgb(255, 153, 51)`, `hsl(30, 100%, 60%)` and the rest, ready to paste into CSS, a design tool or a print brief.

## The main colour formats, explained simply

Screens make colour by mixing red, green and blue light. Every format below is just a different way of writing that mix.

| Format | Example | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HEX | `#4F46E5` | CSS, design handoff, brand guides |
| RGB | `rgb(79, 70, 229)` | Reading values, transparency with `rgba` |
| HSL | `hsl(243, 75%, 59%)` | Adjusting lightness, building palettes |
| HSV / HSB | `hsv(243, 69%, 90%)` | Colour pickers in Photoshop and Figma |
| CMYK | `cmyk(66%, 69%, 0%, 10%)` | A starting point for print |

**HEX** is RGB in hexadecimal: two digits each for red, green and blue, from `00` to `FF` (0 to 255). Short forms like `#FFF` expand to `#FFFFFF`, and an eight-digit form like `#4F46E580` adds transparency.

**HSL** stands for hue (the position on the colour wheel, 0–360 degrees), saturation (how vivid, 0–100%) and lightness (from black at 0% to white at 100%). It is the most intuitive format for making related colours.

**HSV**, also called HSB, uses value or brightness instead of lightness. Many design apps show it in their pickers, so the converter includes it for easy matching.

**CMYK** is the ink model used in printing: cyan, magenta, yellow and black.

## Converting HEX to RGB by hand

It is worth knowing how it works, if only to sanity-check a value. Split the HEX code into pairs and convert each from base 16 to base 10:

```text
#FF9933
 FF -> 15×16 + 15 = 255   (red)
 99 ->  9×16 +  9 = 153   (green)
 33 ->  3×16 +  3 =  51   (blue)
= rgb(255, 153, 51)
```

In JavaScript:

```js
const hex = 'FF9933';
const [r, g, b] = [0, 2, 4].map(i => parseInt(hex.slice(i, i + 2), 16));
// [255, 153, 51]
```

For other base conversions, such as binary or octal, the [Number Base Converter](https://biscsindia.com/tools/number-base-converter/) does the arithmetic.

## Transparency: rgba, hsla and eight-digit HEX

Sometimes you need a colour you can see through, such as a dark overlay on a hero image so white text stays readable. CSS offers three equivalent ways to add an alpha (opacity) value from 0 (invisible) to 1 (solid): `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5)`, `hsla(0, 0%, 0%, 0.5)` and the eight-digit HEX `#00000080`, where the last two digits are the alpha on the 00–FF scale.

The converter reads all three forms. Paste a semi-transparent colour and the alpha carries through to the RGB and HSL outputs, so you can switch notation without losing it. Keep in mind that contrast ratios for see-through colours depend on whatever sits behind them, so check the final, blended result on the real page.

## Why contrast matters

A colour can look great on a brand board and still be unreadable as a button label. Colour vision deficiency is common, particularly among men, and everyone struggles with low contrast on a phone in bright sunlight.

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) measure contrast as a ratio from 1:1 (no difference) to 21:1 (black on white). The common targets are:

- **4.5:1** for normal text (level AA).
- **3:1** for large text and for important interface elements like input borders and icons (level AA).
- **7:1** for normal text at the stricter AAA level.

The converter shows the ratio of your colour against white and against black, with a pass or fail for each level. If neither passes, darken or lighten the colour using the tints and shades row until one does.

## Building a palette from one brand colour

Most brands start with one or two colours. You need more: a lighter version for backgrounds, a darker one for hover states, and borders in between. The **Tints & shades** row gives you that range in one click.

A practical approach for a small business site:

- Use the base colour for primary buttons and links, only if white text on it passes 4.5:1.
- Use a very light tint for section backgrounds or highlighted boxes.
- Use a darker shade for hover and active states.
- Keep body text near-black, not your brand colour, for readability.

Once you have colours, the [CSS Gradient Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/css-gradient-generator/) can blend two of them into a background.

## Common mistakes with colour codes

- **Forgetting the `#`.** CSS needs `#FF9933`, not `FF9933`.
- **Confusing HSL and HSV.** `hsl(30, 100%, 60%)` and `hsv(30, 100%, 60%)` are different colours. Check which one your tool expects.
- **Trusting CMYK for print without a proof.** On-screen conversion cannot know your printer’s inks and paper.
- **Picking text colour by eye.** Always check the contrast ratio, especially for light greys and pastel brand colours.
- **Copying a colour from a compressed image.** JPEG compression shifts colours slightly. Get official brand values from the source file or brand guide where possible.
