Suppose a coaching institute has an admissions page in three languages: `https://www.example.com/admissions/` in English, `/hi/admissions/` in Hindi and `/bn/admissions/` in Bengali, with the English page as the fallback.

Each of the three pages carries the same four lines: one alternate link for `en-IN`, one for `hi-IN`, one for `bn-IN` and one for `x-default` pointing to the English page. The Hindi page lists itself, the English page and the Bengali page, exactly like the other two. That symmetry is what search engines look for; if any page is missing a line, Google may ignore the relationship for that pair.

## Common hreflang mistakes

- **Missing return links.** If the English page points to the Hindi page, the Hindi page must point back to the English page. Every version should carry the full set, including itself.
- **Relative URLs.** Always use absolute `https://` addresses.
- **Wrong codes.** `in` is not India (it is an old code for Indonesian), `en-UK` is invalid (use `en-GB`), and a country alone is not allowed.
- **Pointing to redirected or noindex pages.** Every URL in the set should be live, indexable and canonical.
- **Canonical conflicts.** Each language version should have a self-referencing canonical, not one pointing to the English page.
- **Machine-translated thin pages.** Hreflang helps users find the right version; it does not make poor translations useful. Have a fluent speaker review important pages.

## Tips for multilingual sites in India

Use a clear URL structure such as `/hi/` and `/bn/` folders, so versions are easy to manage. Set the correct `lang` attribute in each page's `html` tag; the [Meta Tag Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/meta-tag-generator/) lets you pick Indian languages for its language setting. Translate titles and meta descriptions as well as body text, since searchers see those first.

After publishing, inspect a few pages in Google Search Console and check that each version is indexed. Whenever you add a language or a new page, regenerate the set with the [Hreflang Tag Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/hreflang-generator/) and update every version together.

Q: Do I need hreflang if my site is only in English?
A: No. Hreflang is only useful when the same page exists in more than one language or regional version. A single-language site, even one serving all of India, does not need it. Focus on a correct html lang attribute instead.

Q: What is x-default in hreflang?
A: x-default names the page to show users whose language or region does not match any of your listed versions. It is usually your main English page or a language selection page. It is optional but recommended for multilingual sites.

Q: Should I use en-IN or just en?
A: Use en-IN only if you have separate English pages for different regions, such as India and the UK, with different prices or content. If you have a single English version for everyone, the plain language code en is simpler and correct.

Q: Is hreflang a ranking factor?
A: Hreflang does not boost rankings. It helps search engines show the right language version of a page that already ranks, so a Hindi speaker sees your Hindi page instead of the English one. Google treats it as a signal rather than a strict directive.

Q: Can I use both head tags and the sitemap for hreflang?
A: Yes, but you only need one method, and if you use both they must match exactly. Head tags are simpler for small sites; sitemap entries are easier to manage when you have many pages and languages.

## How to Find the HSN or SAC Code for Your Product or Service

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/find-hsn-sac-code-gst/
Tool: HSN & SAC Code Finder (https://biscsindia.com/tools/hsn-code-finder/)

Quick answer: HSN codes classify goods and SAC codes classify services for GST. Search by product or service name, narrow to the right chapter and heading, then confirm the full code and current rate in the official CBIC schedule. BISCS India's free HSN & SAC Code Finder searches HS chapters, common headings and SAC codes offline.

To find the HSN code for a product, search by what the product is (for example, "t-shirt" or "laptop"), identify the right chapter and 4-digit heading, and then take the full 6- or 8-digit code from the official tariff. For services, do the same with SAC codes, which all start with 99. Always confirm the code and its GST rate on the CBIC website before you use it on invoices.

The free [HSN & SAC Code Finder](https://biscsindia.com/tools/hsn-code-finder/) on BISCS India speeds up the first part. It searches 97 chapters, around 700 common headings and over 100 service codes by keyword or number, even with small spelling mistakes, and works entirely in your browser.

## What do HSN and SAC codes look like?

HSN codes get more specific as digits are added:

| Digits | Level | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | Chapter | 61: Articles of apparel and clothing accessories, knitted or crocheted |
| 4 | Heading | 6109: T-shirts, singlets and other vests, knitted |
| 6 | Sub-heading (international HS) | Specific type within 6109 |
| 8 | Tariff item (India) | Used in customs and for exports or imports |

SAC codes for services are usually 6 digits, starting with 99. For example, 9982 is the group for legal and accounting services, and 998211 covers legal advisory and representation in criminal law.

## How to use the BISCS HSN & SAC Code Finder

1. Open the [HSN & SAC Code Finder](https://biscsindia.com/tools/hsn-code-finder/).
2. Type a product, service or code in the search box, such as "mobile phone", "rice", "restaurant" or "8471".
3. Optionally filter to **Goods (HSN)** or **Services (SAC)**.
4. Scan the results: each shows the code, its description and where it sits, such as "HSN heading · Chapter 85".
5. Alternatively, browse the **HS tree** on the side, from Section I (live animals) to Section XXI, and click a chapter to list its headings.
6. Click the **copy** button next to a code to paste it into your invoice or accounting software.

With an empty search box, the finder shows popular codes like 8471 (computers), 8517 (phones and routers) and 996331 (restaurant services) to get you started.

## Example searches and what they return

| You search for | Top result |
|---|---|
| t-shirt | 6109: T-shirts, singlets and other vests, knitted or crocheted |
| laptop | 8471: Automatic data processing machines (computers, laptops) |
| mobile phone | 8517: Telephone sets, including smartphones |
| rice | 1006: Rice |
| restaurant | 996331: Restaurant, café and similar eating services, including takeaway |
| legal | 9982: Legal and accounting services |

These headings point you to the right place. You then pick the exact sub-heading from the CBIC rate schedule or Customs Tariff.

## How many digits do you need on a GST invoice?

The rule under current CBIC notifications depends on your aggregate turnover in the previous financial year:

- **Above ₹5 crore:** 6-digit HSN or SAC on all tax invoices.
- **Up to ₹5 crore:** 4-digit HSN or SAC on B2B tax invoices; optional on B2C invoices.
- **Exporters and importers** generally use the full 8-digit ITC-HS code in shipping documents.

HSN-wise summaries are also reported in GSTR-1, so using consistent codes on every invoice makes return filing easier.

## Goods or services? Tricky cases

Choosing between an HSN and a SAC code is usually obvious, but a few situations catch people out:

- **Restaurants and takeaways** supply a service, so they use SAC 996331, even though the customer receives food.
- **Repairs and maintenance** are services. A shop that repairs laptops uses a SAC code, such as 998713, for the labour, and an HSN code for any spare parts it sells separately on the invoice.
- **Software** can be goods or a service depending on how it is supplied, for example packaged media versus a subscription or development work.
- **Construction** is generally a service under SAC group 9954, while selling building materials alone is a supply of goods.
- **Job work** on someone else's goods is a service, even though the result is a physical product.

Where an invoice mixes goods and services, each line needs its own code. If one supply naturally bundles several items, GST has rules for composite and mixed supplies that decide which rate applies; this is worth confirming with a practitioner.

## Why the finder does not show GST rates

GST rates were rationalised with effect from 22 September 2025, with most goods and services moving into the 5% and 18% slabs and a 40% rate for certain luxury and sin goods. Rates for specific items continue to change by notification. Rather than risk showing a stale rate, the finder focuses on getting the code right. Once you have it, look up the rate on the CBIC website and use the [GST Calculator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/gst-calculator/) to work out the tax.

## Tips for choosing the right code

- **Describe what the item is, not what it is used for.** Classification is mainly by material and nature.
- **Prefer the more specific heading** when two seem to fit.
- **Check your suppliers' invoices.** They often show the HSN for the same goods, though you should still verify it.
- **Keep a product master.** Record each product's HSN once and reuse it in the [Invoice Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/invoice-generator/).

## Common mistakes

1. **Using a SAC code for goods or vice versa.**
2. **Showing only 4 digits when your turnover requires 6.**
3. **Copying a rate along with an old code** from a pre-September 2025 invoice.
4. **Guessing from a similar product** instead of checking the heading's description.
5. **Forgetting to validate the customer's GSTIN** on B2B invoices; the [GSTIN Validator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/gstin-validator/) does this quickly.

## Limits of the finder

The finder is an offline guide with HS chapters, common headings and service codes. It is not the full Customs Tariff, does not list every 6- or 8-digit sub-heading, and does not decide classification disputes. This article is general information, not legal or tax advice. Verify codes and rates on the CBIC website and the GST portal, and for doubtful or high-value classifications, consult a GST practitioner or consider an advance ruling.

Q: How many digits of HSN do I need on my invoice?
A: Under the current notification, businesses with aggregate turnover above ₹5 crore in the previous financial year must show a 6-digit HSN or SAC on all tax invoices. Those with turnover up to ₹5 crore must show 4 digits on B2B invoices, while it is optional on B2C invoices. Check the latest CBIC notification.

Q: What is the difference between HSN and SAC?
A: HSN (Harmonised System of Nomenclature) is an international system for classifying goods, organised into chapters and headings. SAC (Services Accounting Code) is India's classification for services under GST, and all SAC codes begin with 99. Goods use HSN and services use SAC on invoices and returns.

Q: Does the finder show GST rates for each code?
A: No. GST rates were rationalised from 22 September 2025 and continue to be revised by notification, so showing rates offline risks giving outdated information. Use the finder to identify the right code, then confirm the current rate on the CBIC GST rate pages before billing.

Q: What if my product fits more than one HSN code?
A: Classification follows the General Rules of Interpretation of the Harmonised System, which look at the specific description, the essential character of the product and other tests. If two headings seem to fit, the more specific one usually applies. For high-value or disputed items, ask a GST practitioner or consider an advance ruling.

Q: Why does the finder only show 4-digit HSN headings?
A: The finder lists all 97 HS chapters, around 700 common 4-digit headings and over 100 SAC groups and codes, which is enough to find the right area quickly. Six- and eight-digit sub-headings run into thousands and are best taken from the Customs Tariff or the CBIC rate schedule.

## HTML Entities: How to Escape and Unescape Special Characters

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/html-entities-escape-unescape-guide/
Tool: HTML Entity Encoder (https://biscsindia.com/tools/html-entity-encoder/)

Quick answer: HTML escaping replaces characters with special meaning in HTML, mainly <, >, & and quotes, with entities such as &lt; and &amp; so browsers show them as text instead of treating them as code. BISCS India's HTML Entity Encoder escapes and unescapes text in named, decimal or hex style, entirely in your browser.

HTML entities are short codes that let you show special characters as plain text on a web page. The browser reads `<` as the start of a tag, so to display a literal less-than sign you write `&lt;`. Escaping is the process of swapping such characters for entities; unescaping turns them back.

The [HTML Entity Encoder](https://biscsindia.com/tools/html-entity-encoder/) on BISCS India does both directions in your browser. It can encode just the essential characters, or every non-ASCII character too, in named, decimal or hexadecimal style.

## Why do some characters need escaping?

HTML uses a handful of characters as syntax. If they appear in your content unescaped, the browser may misread the page:

| Character | Entity | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `&` | `&amp;` | Starts every entity |
| `<` | `&lt;` | Starts a tag |
| `>` | `&gt;` | Ends a tag |
| `"` | `&quot;` | Ends a double-quoted attribute |
| `'` | `&#39;` | Ends a single-quoted attribute |

Suppose you are writing a blog post that shows a code sample. If you paste the raw markup into your page, the browser renders a button rather than displaying the code. Escaped, it shows exactly what you typed:

```html
<!-- What you want readers to see -->
<button class="pay">Pay ₹499</button>

<!-- What you put in the HTML source -->
&lt;button class=&quot;pay&quot;&gt;Pay ₹499&lt;/button&gt;
```

## How to escape or unescape HTML with BISCS India

1. Open the [HTML Entity Encoder](https://biscsindia.com/tools/html-entity-encoder/).
2. Choose **Encode** to escape, or **Decode** to turn entities back into characters.
3. For encoding, set the options:
   - **Encode quotes** (on by default) escapes `"` and `'`, needed for attribute values.
   - **Encode all non-ASCII** also converts characters like ₹, é or Hindi letters into entities.
   - **Style** picks **Named where possible**, **Decimal** (`&#8377;`) or **Hex** (`&#x20B9;`).
4. Paste your text into **Input**. The **Output** updates instantly, with a count of how many entities were created or decoded.
5. Click **Copy**, or **Swap** to reverse the direction and check a round trip.

## Named, decimal and hex entities

The same character can be written three ways. The copyright sign, for example:

```text
&copy;     named
&#169;     decimal code point
&#xA9;     hexadecimal code point
```

Named entities are easier to read, but they exist only for a fixed list of characters. The rupee sign has no widely supported named entity, so it is written as `&#8377;` or `&#x20B9;`. Numeric entities work for any Unicode character, including emoji.

## When should you encode all non-ASCII characters?

For a modern website served as UTF-8, you usually do not need to. You can type ₹, नमस्ते or ধন্যবাদ straight into the HTML. Encoding everything just makes the source harder to read.

Encoding all non-ASCII characters is useful when:

- An email template or older CMS field corrupts special characters.
- You are pasting HTML into a system whose character encoding you do not control.
- You need source files that contain only ASCII for a legacy toolchain.

## Where escaping comes up in everyday work

You do not have to be a security engineer to need this. Some very ordinary situations:

- **Writing tutorials or documentation.** Any page that shows HTML, XML or JSX examples needs the angle brackets escaped, or the browser will try to render them.
- **Pasting content into a CMS.** Some WordPress fields, e-commerce product descriptions and newsletter builders treat input as raw HTML. A product title like `Kurta <Size M> & Dupatta` can silently lose the part in angle brackets.
- **Building XML feeds.** Sitemaps, RSS feeds and product feeds for marketplaces are XML, which is even stricter than HTML. A bare `&` in a product name, such as `Tea & Snacks`, makes the whole feed invalid.
- **Reading scraped or exported data.** Text pulled from web pages or APIs often arrives full of `&amp;`, `&#39;` and `&quot;`. Decoding it gives you clean, readable text before you put it in a spreadsheet or report.
- **Email templates.** HTML emails are rendered by many different clients. Using entities for symbols like ₹ and © is a safe habit when you cannot be sure every client respects UTF-8.

In each case, the fix takes seconds: paste the text, copy the escaped or unescaped version, and move on.

## Escaping and security (XSS)

Cross-site scripting (XSS) happens when an attacker gets their own script to run on your page, usually by submitting text that your site later inserts into HTML without escaping. A comment field containing a script tag, displayed raw, would execute in every visitor’s browser.

Escaping `<`, `>`, `&` and quotes before inserting user text into HTML turns that attack into harmless visible text. But a few cautions apply:

- **Context matters.** Escaping for an HTML text node is not enough for values placed inside a `href`, a `style` or a `<script>` block. Each context has its own rules.
- **Use your framework.** React, Angular, Django, Laravel and most templating engines escape output by default. Bypassing that, for example with `innerHTML` or `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, is where bugs creep in.
- **This tool is for content, not a security layer.** It is ideal for preparing code samples, fixing CMS content or debugging, not for sanitising user input in a live application.

In plain JavaScript, the safe way to insert user text is to set `textContent` rather than `innerHTML`:

```js
el.textContent = userComment;   // shown as text, never run as HTML
```

## Common mistakes

- **Double escaping.** `&amp;amp;` on a page means something escaped twice. Decode once and fix the pipeline.
- **Forgetting the ampersand in URLs.** Query strings in `href` attributes should technically have `&` written as `&amp;`. Browsers forgive this, but validators flag it.
- **Escaping inside code fences in Markdown.** Most Markdown renderers escape code blocks for you. Escaping manually as well gives you visible `&lt;` on the page.
- **Using entities for spacing.** A run of `&nbsp;` to indent text is fragile. Use CSS margin or padding instead.
- **Assuming escaping equals sanitising.** Escaping makes HTML inert; sanitising removes dangerous parts while keeping some formatting. They are different jobs.

## Related tools

If you are cleaning up a page before publishing, the [CSS / HTML / JSON Minifier](https://biscsindia.com/tools/code-minifier/) can compress the final HTML. For characters in links rather than page content, use [URL Encode / Decode](https://biscsindia.com/tools/url-encoder/), because URLs use percent-encoding, not HTML entities. And [Markdown Preview](https://biscsindia.com/tools/markdown-preview/) is handy for checking how escaped text will render in Markdown-based docs.

## Privacy

All conversion happens in your browser with JavaScript. Whatever you paste, whether email templates, internal pages or client copy, stays on your device.

Q: Which characters must be escaped in HTML?
A: At minimum, escape the ampersand as &amp;, the less-than sign as &lt; and the greater-than sign as &gt; in text. Inside attribute values, also escape double quotes as &quot; and single quotes as &#39;. Other characters such as ₹ or Hindi letters can be written directly if the page uses UTF-8.

Q: Does escaping HTML prevent XSS attacks?
A: Escaping untrusted text before inserting it into HTML is a core defence against cross-site scripting, but it must match the context. Text in an element body, an attribute, a URL and inline JavaScript each need different handling. Use your framework’s built-in escaping or templating rather than doing it by hand in production.

Q: What is the difference between named and numeric entities?
A: Named entities use a memorable word, such as &copy; for the copyright sign. Numeric entities use the character’s Unicode code point in decimal, like &#169;, or hexadecimal, like &#xA9;. All three display the same character. Numeric entities work for every character, while named ones exist only for a defined list.

Q: Do I need entities for ₹ or Indian-language text?
A: Not if your page is saved and served as UTF-8 with a meta charset tag, which is standard today. You can type ₹, Devanagari or Tamil directly. Entities like &#8377; are useful when an old system, email template or CMS field mangles non-ASCII characters.

Q: Why does my page show &amp;amp; instead of &?
A: The text was escaped twice. The first pass turned & into &amp;, and the second pass escaped that ampersand again. Decode the text once with the Decode mode, then make sure only one layer of your code performs escaping.

## HEX, RGB or HSL: which code should you use?

| Format | Example | Where it is used |
|---|---|---|
| HEX | #F76B15 | Websites, CSS, Canva-style design tools, most colour fields |
| RGB | rgb(247, 107, 21) | CSS, spreadsheets, programming, some print-shop forms |

If a tool asks for a colour and you are not sure, try HEX first. It is the most widely accepted. To convert between these and other formats, the [Color Converter](https://biscsindia.com/tools/color-converter/) handles it in both directions.

## Picking accurately: what affects the result

### Choose a flat area

A logo on a white background is easy. A red saree in a photo is not: folds, highlights and shadows create dozens of shades of red. Use the magnifier to find a mid-tone area that is neither in shadow nor catching the light.

### Prefer the original file

JPG compression introduces small colour variations, especially around edges and text. A PNG screenshot or the original logo file will give more reliable codes than a photo forwarded several times on WhatsApp.

### Pick a few times and compare

The history row makes it easy to pick three or four nearby points and see how much they vary. If they are very close, any of them will do. If they differ a lot, the area is not a single colour, and the dominant palette may be more useful.

## Using the dominant colour palette

The palette is created by grouping similar pixels in a scaled-down copy of your image with a k-means clustering method. Each swatch shows the colour and the share of the picture it covers.

This is useful when you want the overall feel of an image rather than one exact pixel:

- **Matching a website or social post to a product photo.** Pull the palette from your best product image and use those colours for buttons, backgrounds and text.
- **Wedding and event invitations.** Extract colours from a photo of the venue or the outfit and build a coordinated card.
- **Home décor.** Snap a picture of a cushion or a painting and use the palette to choose wall or curtain colours, then take the codes to the shop. Note that paint on a wall never looks exactly like a screen, so check physical samples too.

The **Copy CSS variables** button gives you lines such as `--color-1: #...;`, ready for a stylesheet. Pair them with the [CSS Gradient Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/css-gradient-generator/) to build backgrounds that blend two palette colours.

## Building a colour scheme from one picked colour

Often you only need one starting colour, and the rest can be derived from it. This is where the HSL code is handy. Keep the hue the same and change the lightness to get a family of matching shades: a darker version for text or buttons, a much lighter version for backgrounds, and the original for highlights.

Say you run a small sweet shop and your signboard orange picks as roughly hsl(23, 93%, 53%). A version at 35% lightness works for headings, the original for buttons, and a pale 94% version for page or poster backgrounds. Because they share a hue, they always look like they belong together.

For a contrasting accent, move the hue roughly halfway round the colour wheel, about 180 degrees. Orange pairs with a deep blue, for example. Test text colours for readability on their backgrounds before finalising anything for print or a website.

## Common mistakes

- **Picking from an anti-aliased edge.** The pixels where a letter meets the background are a blend of both. Pick from the middle of a shape.
- **Trusting a photo of a printed colour.** Camera white balance and room lighting change colours a lot. For accurate brand colours, use the digital artwork or the official guidelines.
- **Ignoring screen differences.** The code is exact, but how it looks varies between phone screens, laptops and printers.
- **Mixing up similar codes.** When copying several colours, label them in your notes so you do not paste the shadow tone instead of the main one.

## Your images stay private

The image is read and analysed by your browser on your own device. Nothing is uploaded, so you can safely pick colours from unreleased designs, client mock-ups or internal dashboards. Very large photos are analysed on a reduced copy for the palette, which keeps it quick even on phones, while individual picks use the full-resolution pixels.

Q: Why is the picked colour slightly different from my brand colour?
A: Photos and screenshots rarely contain one perfectly flat colour. Lighting, shadows, JPG compression and screen colour profiles all shift pixels slightly. Pick from the flattest, best-lit area, use the magnifier, and compare a few nearby points. For official brand colours, ask for the brand guidelines.

Q: What is the difference between HEX, RGB and HSL?
A: They describe the same colour in different ways. HEX is a six-character code such as #F76B15 used in web design. RGB lists red, green and blue amounts from 0 to 255. HSL uses hue, saturation and lightness, which is handy when you want a lighter or darker shade.

Q: How does the dominant colour palette work?
A: The tool scans a reduced copy of your image and groups similar pixels together using a clustering method called k-means. Each group becomes one colour in the palette, shown with the percentage of the image it covers. You can choose five, six, eight or ten colours.

Q: Can I pick colours from a screenshot of a website or app?
A: Yes. Take a screenshot, then paste it straight into the tool with Ctrl + V or upload the file. Screenshots are usually PNG, which keeps colours exact, so the codes you pick from flat buttons and backgrounds are generally very accurate.

Compressing an image means making its file smaller, measured in KB or MB, while keeping it looking as close to the original as possible. You need it when a form rejects a photo for being too large, when an email bounces because of attachment size, or when a website loads slowly because of heavy pictures.

The [Compress Image](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-compressor/) tool from BISCS India handles JPG, PNG and WebP. You can either set a quality level yourself or type a target such as 50 KB and let the tool work out the best settings that fit.

## How does image compression actually work?

There are three ways to make an image file smaller, and good compressors combine them:

1. **Lower the encoding quality.** JPG and WebP throw away fine detail the eye barely notices. A quality of 75% often halves the file with no visible change.
2. **Reduce the dimensions.** A 4000 × 3000 photo has 12 million pixels. At 1600 × 1200 it has under 2 million, so even at the same quality the file is far smaller.
3. **Use a more efficient format.** A camera photo saved as PNG can be several times larger than the same photo as JPG. WebP is usually smaller still.

The target size mode in the BISCS India tool searches through quality levels to find the best one under your limit. Only if quality alone cannot get there does it start reducing the dimensions.

## Step by step: compress a photo to a target size

1. Open [Compress Image](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-compressor/) and add your photos. You can drop in several at once or paste an image with Ctrl + V.
2. Choose the mode at the top of the panel:
   - **Quality** if you just want smaller files and are happy to set the slider yourself.
   - **Target size** if a portal or app gives you a KB limit.
3. In Target size mode, type the limit in KB or tap a chip: 20 KB, 50 KB, 100 KB, 200 KB, 500 KB or 1 MB.
4. Optionally set a **Max width / height**, such as 1920 px for websites or 1280 px for email.
5. Pick the **Output format**. Auto keeps JPG for photos, uses WebP for images with transparency, and converts opaque PNGs to JPG.
6. Drag the comparison slider across the preview to check quality, read the before and after sizes, and download. Batches download as a ZIP.

## Quality settings and what to expect

| Quality setting | Typical use | What you will notice |
|---|---|---|
| 85–95% | Portfolios, printing, product hero shots | Practically identical to the original |
| 65–80% | Websites, WhatsApp, email, most forms | Hard to tell apart on screen; big savings |
| 40–60% | Very strict upload limits | Softer detail, some blockiness in plain areas |
| Below 40% | Last resort only | Visible artefacts, colour banding, smudged text |

## Compressing photos and signatures for Indian application forms

Recruitment and admission portals, such as those for SSC, UPSC, IBPS and other bank exams, state public service commissions and university admissions, almost always set a size range in KB for the photograph and the signature. Often there is both a minimum and a maximum, and sometimes fixed pixel dimensions as well.

These limits are not the same everywhere, and they change between notifications. Always read the current official notice or the portal’s upload instructions before you start, rather than relying on a number you saw on a forum.

A reliable workflow:

1. Crop the photo so the face is well framed, using [Crop Image](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-cropper/).
2. If dimensions are specified, set them exactly with [Resize Image](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-resizer/).
3. Compress with Target size set a little below the maximum, for example a few KB under it, to leave a safety margin.
4. Check that the result is above the minimum. If it is not, raise the target or the quality.
5. Make sure the format matches what the portal accepts, which is usually JPG.

The same approach works for scanned signatures, caste or income certificates saved as images, and thumb impressions.

## Practical tips

- **Start from the best original.** Compressing a photo that WhatsApp has already compressed piles new losses on old ones. Use the original camera file where possible.
- **Crop before you compress.** Removing empty wall or sky reduces the pixels the compressor has to fit into your limit, so the important part keeps more quality.
- **Screenshots are special.** Text-heavy screenshots look best as PNG or at high JPG quality. If they must be tiny, reduce the width rather than crushing the quality.
- **Watch the Saved figure.** If a file shows “Already optimised”, it was already efficient and further squeezing would only make it worse.
- **For PDFs, use a different tool.** If you need a smaller PDF rather than a smaller image, [Compress PDF](https://biscsindia.com/tools/compress-pdf/) is designed for that.

## Common mistakes

- **Aiming exactly at the limit.** Some portals count KB slightly differently. A file of exactly the maximum can still be rejected, so leave a small margin.
- **Compressing again and again.** Each pass at low quality adds more damage. If the result is too big, go back to the original and set a smaller target.
- **Ignoring the minimum size.** A 6 KB photo for a form that wants at least 20 KB will be refused just as firmly as an oversized one.
- **Choosing PNG for a photo and wondering why it will not shrink.** Switch to JPG or Auto.
- **Over-compressing a signature.** Thin pen strokes break up at low quality. Crop tightly and keep quality reasonable instead.

## Does it work offline and is it private?

The compression runs in your browser using its built-in image encoder. Your photos are not uploaded to any server, so personal pictures, ID scans and documents stay on your device. Large batches of high-resolution photos may take a little longer on an older phone, simply because the work is being done locally rather than on a remote machine.

Q: How do I reduce a photo to under 50 KB for a form?
A: Switch the compressor to Target size, type 50 or tap the 50 KB chip, and download. The tool tries different quality levels to find the best one that fits. If even the lowest sensible quality is too big, it reduces the pixel dimensions slightly as well.

Q: Why can’t the tool reach my target size?
A: Very small targets for very large or detailed images may be impossible without destroying the picture. The tool then gives you the smallest version it could make and tells you. Resizing to smaller dimensions first, or cropping away empty space, usually solves it.

Q: Will compression make my photo look blurry?
A: At moderate settings, around 60 to 80 percent quality, most photos look the same as the original on a phone or laptop screen. Problems appear at very low quality: blocky skies, smudged edges and colour banding. Use the before-and-after slider to judge for yourself.

Q: Why does my PNG barely get smaller?
A: PNG is lossless, so the quality slider has no effect on it. Large savings come from converting photos to JPG or WebP, or from reducing the maximum width. The Auto format option handles this by converting opaque PNG photos to JPG automatically.

Q: Is my photo too small if the form has a minimum size?
A: Some portals set a minimum as well as a maximum KB value. If your compressed file is below the minimum, raise the quality or choose a larger target size rather than enlarging the image. A higher quality JPG of the same dimensions will weigh more.

## JPG, PNG or WebP: which format should you use?

Each format was designed for a different job. Choosing the right one matters more than any quality slider.

| Format | Best for | Transparency | Typical file size | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| JPG (JPEG) | Photos, form uploads, printing | No | Small | Text and sharp edges can blur slightly |
| PNG | Screenshots, logos, graphics, cut-outs | Yes | Large for photos | Big files when used for camera photos |
| WebP | Websites and apps | Yes | Smallest | A few older portals and programs still reject it |

A simple rule: photos go to JPG (or WebP for websites), anything with flat colours, text or a transparent background goes to PNG.

## Common conversions and when they make sense

### PNG to JPG

This is the most common one. Phone screenshots and some scanner apps save as PNG, which can be several megabytes for a single image. Many exam and job portals in India only accept JPG for photo and signature uploads. Converting fixes both issues in one step.

If the PNG has a transparent background, such as a signature cut-out, the transparent area must become a solid colour in JPG. Choose white for forms.

### JPG to PNG

Converting a JPG to PNG does **not** improve its quality. The compression artefacts already in the JPG stay there, and the file usually grows. It makes sense only when the next program in your workflow requires PNG, or you plan to edit the image repeatedly and do not want further JPG losses each time you save.

### Anything to WebP

If you run a website, an online shop or a blog, WebP is usually the most efficient choice for both photos and graphics, and it supports transparency. Page speed matters for visitors on mobile data, so converting your product images to WebP is a worthwhile habit.

### WebP to JPG

Images saved from websites often turn out to be WebP. When an older desktop program, a print shop or a government portal refuses the file, converting it to JPG solves the problem straight away.

## What happens to quality when you convert?

JPG and WebP are **lossy**: they discard detail the eye is unlikely to notice. The quality slider controls how much is thrown away. At very low settings you will see blocky patches in skies and smudged edges around text.

PNG is **lossless**: it stores every pixel exactly. That is why the quality slider does not apply to PNG output, and why PNG photos are large.

Converting from a lossy format to a lossless one cannot bring back lost detail. Converting the other way, PNG to JPG, loses a little each time. For important images, keep the original file and convert from that rather than converting a converted copy.

## Tips for clean conversions

- **Use the right tool for size targets.** If a form says the photo must be under a certain number of KB, use [Compress Image](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-compressor/), which searches for the quality that fits. Converting alone may not land on the number.
- **Check dimensions too.** Converting does not change width and height. If the portal also specifies pixels, use [Resize Image](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-resizer/) first.
- **Keep logos in PNG.** Converting a logo with crisp edges to JPG tends to add faint halos. PNG or WebP keep it clean.
- **Batch your work.** If you are preparing thirty product photos for a website, add them all at once and download a ZIP rather than converting one at a time.
- **Animated GIFs become still images.** The converter works on a single frame, so an animation will not survive conversion to JPG or PNG.

## Common mistakes

- Converting a JPG to PNG expecting it to look sharper. It will not, and the file will be bigger.
- Saving a transparent logo as JPG and getting a black or white box around it.
- Uploading WebP to a portal that only lists JPG and PNG, then wondering why the upload button greys out.
- Setting quality to 100% for every photo. The file grows a lot for almost no visible gain over 90%.
- Renaming a file from `.png` to `.jpg` by hand. That changes the label, not the content, and some portals will detect the mismatch.

Yes. The BISCS India converter uses your browser’s own image encoding, so the file is read and rewritten on your phone or computer. Nothing is uploaded, which matters if you are converting scanned certificates, ID cards or client work. When you have finished, you can turn the result into a PDF with [JPG to PDF](https://biscsindia.com/tools/jpg-to-pdf/) if the portal wants a document rather than an image.

Q: Does converting PNG to JPG reduce quality?
A: Slightly, because JPG uses lossy compression. At a quality of around 90% the difference is very hard to see in photos. Screenshots with sharp text can show faint smudges around letters, so keep those as PNG if crispness matters more than file size.

Q: Why did the transparent background turn white after converting to JPG?
A: JPG has no support for transparency, so every transparent pixel must be given a solid colour. The converter lets you choose that background colour. If you need to keep the transparency, convert to PNG or WebP instead, both of which support it.

Q: How do I open a WebP image that will not upload to a form?
A: Some older websites and government portals only accept JPG or PNG. Add the WebP file to the converter, choose JPG as the target format and download. The new file will open and upload anywhere that accepts ordinary photos.

Q: Can I convert HEIC iPhone photos with this tool?
A: The converter reads any image format your browser can open. Most browsers on Windows and Android cannot decode HEIC, so it may not load there. On an iPhone, sharing the photo as Most Compatible or changing the camera setting to JPG avoids the problem.

Q: Is converting the format the same as compressing the image?
A: Not exactly, but they are related. Converting a PNG photo to JPG or WebP usually makes it much smaller, because those formats compress photos better. If you need to reach a specific KB limit, use the compressor, which can search for the right quality automatically.

An aspect ratio is simply width compared to height. Picking the right one before you crop saves you from having the platform crop your picture for you, often in the wrong place.

| Aspect ratio | Shape | Common uses |
|---|---|---|
| Free | Any | Removing clutter, trimming screenshots, documents |

## Tips for a better crop

### Use the rule of thirds

The grid divides the frame into nine parts. Placing a person’s eyes on the upper line, or the horizon on the lower or upper line rather than the middle, tends to look more natural. For product photos and passport-style shots, centring is better.

### Leave breathing room

Cropping right up to the edge of someone’s head or chin looks cramped. Leave a little space above the head and keep the chin clear. If you are cropping for an official photo, follow the specific head-size guidance of the authority concerned.

### Watch the pixel count

Every crop throws pixels away. A tight crop from a 12-megapixel photo is still large, but a tight crop from a WhatsApp image might leave only a few hundred pixels, which will look soft when printed or enlarged. The result preview tells you the final size before you download.

### Straighten first

If the horizon is tilted, crop alone will not fix it. Straighten the photo with the fine-angle control in [Rotate & Flip Image](https://biscsindia.com/tools/rotate-flip-image/), then crop away the angled edges.

## Tips for natural-looking edits

### Fix light before colour

Get brightness and contrast right first. Colour adjustments look different on a dark photo than on a well-exposed one, so tuning saturation before brightness often means doing it twice.

### Go easy on saturation

Skin tones are the first thing to suffer. If faces start to look orange or red, pull saturation back. For portraits, warmth from the Warm preset often flatters more than raw saturation.

### Use hue for colour casts, gently

Photos under tube lights can turn greenish, and some indoor bulbs make everything yellow. A hue shift of just a few degrees can neutralise that. Large hue shifts make skin look unnatural.

### Keep a consistent look across a set

If you are editing photos for a shop catalogue, a wedding album or an Instagram grid, note the slider values that worked on the first picture and apply the same ones to the rest. Consistency looks more professional than a different filter on every image.

## Editing for social media and online shops

On Instagram or Facebook, a slightly brighter, slightly more vivid image tends to look better in a busy feed, because phone screens show colour well and posts are viewed small. The Vivid preset with brightness pulled back a little is a reliable starting point for food, clothing and travel photos.

For an online shop on a marketplace or your own website, accuracy matters more than drama. A customer who orders a maroon kurta and receives something that looks brown will be unhappy. Keep saturation close to normal, correct only obvious colour casts, and compare the edited photo with the real product in daylight. Use the same settings for every product photo in a collection so the colours look consistent next to each other.

## When filters are not the right tool

Filters change the overall look of a picture. They are not designed for:

- **Old, faded or noisy photos** that need dust removal, colour-cast correction and sharpening. The [Photo Enhancer](https://biscsindia.com/tools/ai-photo-enhancer/) is built for that.
- **Blurring only the background** behind a person. Use the [AI Background Blur & Changer](https://biscsindia.com/tools/ai-background-changer/), which separates the subject first.
- **Artistic effects** such as sketches, cartoons or pop-art. Try [Photo Art Effects](https://biscsindia.com/tools/photo-art-effects/).

## Common mistakes

- **Maximum contrast on a photo with a bright sky.** The clouds turn pure white and lose all detail.
- **Heavy vignette on group photos.** People at the edges end up in the dark.
- **Editing on a very dim screen.** Your photo will look too bright on everyone else’s phone. Check it at normal brightness.
- **Using filters on documents for official upload.** Sepia, vintage or blur effects on an ID scan or certificate can lead to rejection. For documents, only use brightness and contrast to improve readability, or try B&W.
- **Applying a filter, saving, and filtering again.** Each JPG save loses a little quality. Make all your adjustments in one session.

## Your photos stay on your device

The filters are applied using your browser’s own graphics features. Your photo is not uploaded, so there is no risk of personal pictures being stored on someone else’s server. If your browser lacks the canvas filter feature, the tool switches to a compatibility mode automatically, so the edits still work.

Q: How do I make a photo black and white without it looking flat?
A: Use the B&W or Noir preset rather than just setting saturation to zero. Both add extra contrast, which keeps the picture punchy. Then adjust brightness so the darkest areas are truly dark and the lightest areas are bright but not blown out.

Q: Can photo filters fix a blurry or very dark picture?
A: Filters can lighten a dark photo and add punch to a dull one, but they cannot recover detail that the camera never captured. For noise, colour casts and soft detail, the Photo Enhancer, which includes sharpening and noise reduction, is the better choice.

Q: Do the filters reduce the resolution of my photo?
A: No. The preview may be scaled to fit your screen, but the download is rendered at the photo’s full original size. Only the adjustments you choose are applied, so a 4000 pixel wide photo stays 4000 pixels wide.

Q: What does the vignette slider do?
A: A vignette gently darkens the corners and edges of the picture. It draws the eye towards the centre and gives portraits and moody shots a more finished look. Keep it subtle for everyday photos; strong vignettes quickly look dated.

Q: Can I see the original while I am editing?
A: Yes. Press and hold the Hold to compare button on the preview to see the unedited photo, then release it to return to your edit. It is the quickest way to check you have not overdone the contrast or saturation.

## How to Resize an Image in Pixels or Percentage, Free Online

Resizing an image means changing its width and height in pixels. You do it to make a photo fit a website slot, an Instagram post, a WhatsApp display picture or the exact dimensions an online form asks for. The quickest way is to type the new size, keep the aspect ratio locked so nothing gets stretched, and download.

## When do you actually need to resize a photo?

Most phone cameras now save pictures at 12 megapixels or more, around 4000 × 3000 pixels. That is far more than most uses need, and it causes real problems:

- **Online application forms.** Government recruitment portals, university admissions and bank exam sites often ask for a photo and signature within fixed pixel dimensions. Upload a full-size phone photo and the portal rejects it.
- **Websites and blogs.** A 4000-pixel hero image slows the page down for no visible benefit on a 1920-pixel-wide screen.
- **Social media.** Platforms crop or recompress images that do not match their preferred sizes, sometimes badly.
- **Email and chat.** Smaller images send faster on mobile data and take less space in your recipient’s inbox.

If your problem is the file size in KB rather than the dimensions, you need compression as well. The [Compress Image](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-compressor/) tool can hit a target size such as 50 KB, and it is often best used after resizing.

2. Pick **By pixels** if you know the exact size you need, or **By percentage** if you just want the picture smaller (for example 50%).
3. In pixel mode, type a width. With the lock button on, the height updates automatically so the proportions stay the same.

## Pixels, percentage or preset: which should you use?

| Situation | Best option | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Form asks for a specific width and height | By pixels, with Crop to fill | You get the exact numbers without distorting the face |
| You just want smaller files for WhatsApp or email | By percentage (25–50%) | Quick, keeps proportions, no maths needed |

| Product photos for an online shop | By pixels, same width for all | Gives a consistent grid across your catalogue |
| Making an image larger | Try AI upscaling instead | Plain enlargement cannot invent missing detail |

## Understanding aspect ratio (and why photos get squashed)

The aspect ratio is the relationship between width and height. A typical phone photo is 4:3, so a 4000 × 3000 image resized to 1200 wide becomes 1200 × 900. If you then force it to 1200 × 1200, something has to give.

**Stretch** squeezes the picture into the new box, which makes people look wider or thinner. It is rarely what you want. **Crop to fill** scales the photo until the box is covered and trims the overflow from the edges. **Fit inside** scales the photo until it fits completely and fills the leftover space, so nothing is cut off.

For portraits and passport-style photos, crop to fill usually looks best. For logos, screenshots and documents, fit inside is safer because nothing important gets trimmed. If you want to choose exactly what gets trimmed, crop by hand first with [Crop Image](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-cropper/), then resize.

## Resizing photos for Indian exam and job application forms

Recruitment and admission portals in India commonly ask for a recent colour photograph and a scanned signature, each with its own pixel dimensions, file format and size range in KB. The exact numbers are not universal. They differ between SSC, UPSC, banking, railway and state commission notifications, and they can change from one recruitment cycle to the next.

So before resizing, open the official notification or the portal’s instructions and note three things: the pixel dimensions (if given), the file format (usually JPG) and the minimum and maximum size in KB. Then:

- Resize to the stated dimensions using pixel mode with crop to fill.
- If the result is above the KB limit, run it through the compressor with a target size.
- If it is below the minimum KB, raise the quality during compression rather than enlarging the image.

For signatures, sign in dark ink on plain white paper, photograph it in good light, crop tightly around the signature and then resize. The [Signature Maker](https://biscsindia.com/tools/signature-maker/) can also create a clean digital signature if the form accepts one.

## Practical tips for better results

- **Resize once, from the original.** Every round of resizing and re-saving a JPG loses a little quality. Keep your original and always start from it.
- **Downsizing is safe, upsizing is not.** Going from 4000 to 1200 pixels looks crisp. Going from 400 to 1200 looks blurry because the extra pixels are guessed. For enlargements, the [AI Image Upscaler](https://biscsindia.com/tools/ai-image-upscaler/) reconstructs detail more convincingly.
- **Use even numbers for video and design work.** Some video encoders and layout systems prefer even widths and heights.
- **Mind the format.** Resizing does not change the file type. If you need a JPG from a PNG screenshot, convert it as well.
- **Large batches on a phone take longer.** Everything runs on your device, so a budget phone handling fifty 12-megapixel photos will need a little patience. A laptop is quicker for big jobs.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- Typing both width and height with the lock off and ending up with distorted faces.
- Resizing a photo to the right dimensions but forgetting the KB limit, then getting rejected anyway.
- Enlarging a small WhatsApp-forwarded photo for printing and expecting it to look sharp.
- Cropping out part of the head or chin in an application photo because crop to fill trimmed more than expected. Check the preview before downloading.
- Repeatedly editing and saving the same JPG instead of going back to the original.

## Is it safe to resize personal photos online?

Many online resizers upload your image to their server, process it there and send it back. With the BISCS India resizer, the work happens locally using your browser’s built-in canvas. Your photo, ID scan or signature is never transmitted, so there is nothing stored on someone else’s computer afterwards. Once the page has loaded, the tool continues to work even on a weak connection.

That makes it a sensible choice for Aadhaar or PAN scans, family pictures and anything else you would rather not hand over to an unknown website.

Q: Does resizing an image reduce its quality?
A: Making an image smaller usually looks fine because you are throwing away pixels you do not need. Making it larger cannot add real detail, so a small photo stretched to twice its size will look soft. For enlargements, an AI upscaler gives better results than a plain resize.

Q: What is the difference between resizing and compressing?
A: Resizing changes the pixel dimensions, for example from 4000 × 3000 to 1200 × 900. Compressing keeps the dimensions but stores the pixels more efficiently, which lowers the file size in KB. Forms often specify both, so you may need to resize first and then compress.

Q: Can I resize many photos at the same time?
A: Yes. Add several images together and the same settings are applied to each of them. With the aspect ratio lock on, every photo keeps its own shape based on the width or height you enter, and you can download them all together as a ZIP file.

Q: Why is my resized photo stretched or squashed?
A: That happens when the width and height you type do not match the original shape and the image is forced into them. Keep the lock on, or choose Crop to fill or Fit inside so the tool trims or pads the picture instead of distorting faces and text.

Q: Are my photos uploaded anywhere when I resize them?
A: No. The resizing is done by your browser on your own device using the canvas feature built into every modern browser. The images are not sent to BISCS India or any other server, which makes it suitable for ID scans and personal photos.

## How to Convert an Image to Base64 (Data URL, CSS and HTML)

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/convert-image-to-base64-data-url/
Tool: Image to Base64 (https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-to-base64/)

Quick answer: To convert an image to Base64, open an encoder, choose the image and copy the result as a data URL, raw Base64, CSS background, HTML img tag, Markdown or JSON. BISCS India’s Image to Base64 tool does this in your browser, shows how much larger the encoded text is, and never uploads the file.

Converting an image to Base64 turns the binary file into a long string of plain text characters. Wrapped as a data URL, that text can be pasted straight into HTML, CSS, JSON or Markdown, so the image travels inside the code instead of as a separate file.

The [Image to Base64](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-to-base64/) tool from BISCS India reads your image and gives you the encoded result in six ready-to-use formats. The encoding happens on your device, and you can copy the result or download it as a text file.

## What is a Base64 data URL?

Base64 is a way of writing any binary data using only 64 safe characters: letters, digits, plus and slash. It was designed so that binary files could travel through systems built for text, such as email.

A **data URL** is Base64 with a short header that tells the browser what kind of file it is, for example `data:image/png;base64,` followed by the encoded text. Browsers can display a data URL exactly as if it were a link to an image file.

## How to convert an image to Base64

1. Open [Image to Base64](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-to-base64/) and choose an image, drag it in or paste it with Ctrl + V.
2. Look at the stats: type, dimensions, original file size and the Base64 size with its percentage increase.
3. Pick the output you need:
   - **Data URL**: the full `data:image/...;base64,...` string.
   - **Base64**: just the encoded characters, without the header.
   - **CSS**: a ready `background-image` rule.
   - **HTML img**: an `img` tag with the width and height already filled in.
   - **Markdown**: an image link for README files and notes.
   - **JSON**: an object with name, type, width, height and data.
4. Press **Copy**, or **Download .txt** for very long strings that are awkward to copy on a phone.

## When embedding an image as Base64 makes sense

| Use case | Good idea? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Tiny icons and small UI graphics | Yes | Saves a separate request for a few hundred bytes |
| Single-file HTML pages or reports | Yes | Everything works offline in one file |
| Test data and API payloads | Yes | JSON-friendly, easy to send and store as text |
| Placeholder images while developing | Yes | No need to host files yet |
| Large photos on a website | No | Bloats the page, cannot be cached separately |
| Images reused across many pages | No | Downloaded again inside every page instead of once |
| Hiding or protecting images | No | Anyone can decode Base64 instantly |

As a rule of thumb, Base64 shines for images measured in a few kilobytes. The tool shows a warning when the encoded result becomes large, which is your cue to consider a normal image file instead.

## Practical examples

### Inline icons in a single HTML file

If you are building a self-contained HTML invoice, report or offline page, embedding the logo means the file still shows it when emailed or opened without internet. Small PNG or SVG-style graphics work best.

### Sending an image through an API

Many web APIs accept images as a Base64 field inside JSON. The JSON output gives you a ready object with the data plus useful metadata such as width and height, which saves writing a conversion script for a quick test.

### CSS backgrounds for tiny patterns

A small repeating texture or a loader graphic can live inside your stylesheet. Use the CSS output and paste it into your rules.

## How big is too big?

There is no single cut-off, but it helps to think about what the browser has to do. A normal image file can download in parallel with the rest of the page and be cached for the next visit. A Base64 image inside your HTML or CSS must be downloaded and read before the surrounding code is finished, every single time that code loads.

For icons of a few kilobytes, that cost is negligible and you save a network request. Once an encoded image grows past a few tens of kilobytes, the trade-off usually turns against embedding. That is why the tool warns you when the encoded text becomes large. For developers working on page speed, a mix works well: embed only the tiny, above-the-fold graphics and keep everything else as separate, cacheable files.

## Tips to keep embedded images light

- **Shrink first.** Resize to the dimensions you actually display with [Resize Image](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-resizer/), then compress with [Compress Image](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-compressor/). A 500 KB photo becomes roughly 670 KB of text; a 15 KB optimised version becomes about 20 KB.
- **Choose the right format before encoding.** WebP or a well-compressed JPG is smaller than PNG for photos, and the size difference carries straight through to the Base64 text.
- **Do not embed the same image twice.** If the logo appears in several places, define it once in CSS as a class.
- **Decoding works in reverse.** If you are given a Base64 string and need to inspect general text encodings, the [Base64 Encoder](https://biscsindia.com/tools/base64-encoder/) handles text in both directions.

## Common mistakes

- **Pasting the data URL where only raw Base64 is expected,** or the other way round. APIs often want the raw part without the `data:` header; HTML and CSS need the header.
- **Embedding hero images on a website.** The page appears blank for longer because the browser must download the whole string before showing anything.
- **Treating Base64 as security.** It offers no protection at all.
- **Breaking the string.** Some editors wrap or trim long lines. If an image fails to show, check that nothing was cut off when copying.

## Is it private?

The image is read by your browser and encoded locally. Nothing is uploaded, so you can safely encode screenshots of internal dashboards, client logos or draft designs. The original file is used as it is, without re-compression, so the encoded image is pixel-for-pixel identical to what you selected.

Q: Why is the Base64 version larger than the original image?
A: Base64 represents every three bytes of binary data with four text characters, so the encoded text is roughly a third larger than the file. A data URL also adds a short prefix naming the file type. The tool shows the exact increase for your image.

Q: Is Base64 a way to encrypt or hide an image?
A: No. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Anyone can decode the text back into the original image instantly, without a password. Do not use it to protect private pictures or to hide anything sensitive in web pages or apps.

Q: When should I avoid embedding images as Base64?
A: Avoid it for large photos and for images used on many pages. Embedded images cannot be cached separately by the browser, they make HTML and CSS files heavier, and they delay the rest of the page from loading. Keep them as normal files instead.

Q: Can I use a Base64 image in an email signature?
A: Sometimes. Some email programs display data URL images, but several popular webmail services block or strip them. For email signatures, a small image hosted at a normal web address or attached to the message is usually more reliable across different inboxes.

Image to text, also called OCR (optical character recognition), reads the letters in a picture and turns them into editable text you can copy, search and paste. It saves retyping a notice someone photographed, a page from a book, a screenshot of a message, or an old scanned letter.

## Getting accurate results: what matters most

| Factor | Good | Poor |
|---|---|---|
| Lighting | Even daylight, no shadows | Phone shadow across the page, dim room |
| Angle | Camera directly above the page | Steep angle, curved book pages |
| Focus | Sharp text | Motion blur, out of focus |
| Text size | Letters clearly visible when zoomed | Tiny print far from the camera |
| Font | Standard printed fonts | Handwriting, decorative or stylised fonts |
| Language setting | Only the languages present | Every language ticked “just in case” |

### Photograph documents properly

Hold the phone parallel to the page, fill the frame with the text, tap to focus, and avoid using flash on glossy paper. For multi-page documents photographed at an angle, run them through [Scan to PDF](https://biscsindia.com/tools/scan-to-pdf/) first. It flattens the perspective and cleans the background, which noticeably improves OCR.

### Choose languages carefully

Ticking Hindi when a page is only in English makes the engine consider Devanagari shapes for every letter, which slows it down and can add strange characters. Tick only the scripts you can actually see. For a bilingual form with English and Bengali, tick both.

### Proofread what matters

OCR gives a confidence score, but even a high score does not mean every character is right. Check names, amounts, dates, PAN or account numbers, and anything you will act on. Common confusions include 0 and O, 1 and l, and similar-looking Hindi or Bengali conjuncts.

## Working with PDFs

A PDF can contain real digital text, scanned page images, or both. The tool handles each page appropriately: digital text is taken directly when the option is on, and scanned pages are read with OCR.

If you need the result as an editable Word document instead of plain text, [PDF to Word](https://biscsindia.com/tools/pdf-to-word/) can convert the layout and use OCR for scanned pages. For PDFs that are entirely digital, [PDF to Text](https://biscsindia.com/tools/pdf-to-text/) is quicker.

## Turning extracted text into something useful

Once you have the text, a few other tools help you finish the job quickly:

- **Count or trim it.** If you are adapting a printed passage for an assignment or a social post, the [Word Counter](https://biscsindia.com/tools/word-counter/) shows words, characters and reading time.
- **Listen to it.** For long notices or study material, [Text to Speech](https://biscsindia.com/tools/text-to-speech/) reads the text aloud, which helps when proofreading too.
- **Clean up spacing.** OCR output sometimes contains extra line breaks where the original page wrapped. Join lines in your editor, or paste the text into a document and reflow it.
- **Move numbers into a spreadsheet.** For bills and statements, copy the relevant lines, paste them into a sheet, and split them into columns.

Keep the original image alongside the text, especially for official documents. If there is ever a question about what the paper said, the image is the record; the OCR text is a convenience copy.

## Common mistakes

- **Uploading a blurry WhatsApp forward.** WhatsApp compresses images; ask for the original or a sharper photo.
- **Leaving the page curved.** The text near a book’s spine bends and gets misread. Press the page flat.
- **Expecting table layout.** OCR gives you the text in reading order, not a formatted table. You may need to tidy columns in a spreadsheet.
- **Trusting numbers without checking.** A single wrong digit in a bank account or invoice number matters.
- **Ticking all languages for an English screenshot.** It slows things down and can reduce accuracy.

## Private OCR, on your device

Many OCR websites upload your images to their servers. This tool uses the open-source Tesseract engine running in your browser, with the engine and language data served from this site and stored by your browser after the first use. Your documents, whether bank statements, medical reports or personal letters, stay on your device. Very long PDFs take time on a phone, so a laptop is more comfortable for big jobs.

Q: How accurate is OCR on Hindi and Bengali text?
A: Clear printed Hindi and Bengali text, such as newspapers, books and typed documents, is usually read well. Accuracy drops with handwriting, decorative fonts, very small text and low-quality photos. Always proofread the result, especially names, numbers and matras or conjuncts, which are easy to misread.

Q: Can it read handwritten notes?
A: The OCR engine is designed for printed text. Neat handwriting in block letters sometimes works partly, but joined or casual handwriting usually produces many errors. For handwritten notes, typing them out or using a dedicated handwriting recognition service is more reliable.

Q: What is a searchable PDF?
A: A searchable PDF looks like the original scan but contains an invisible layer of recognised text. You can then search it with Ctrl + F, select and copy text, and let computers index it. It is useful for archiving scanned bills, letters and certificates.

Q: Why is the first run slower?
A: The first time you use a language, your browser downloads the OCR engine and that language’s data, then stores them. Later runs load from the browser’s cache and start much faster. Ticking only the languages actually present also speeds things up and improves accuracy.

Q: Can I extract text from a PDF that is not scanned?
A: Yes. If a PDF already contains digital text, the tool can use that text directly, which is faster and exact, while still running OCR on any scanned pages. For digital PDFs without scanned pages, the PDF to Text tool is a simpler option.

## Watermarking ID copies before sharing them
