A text compare tool, often called a diff checker, shows exactly what changed between two versions of a text. Paste the original on the left and the new version on the right. Lines that were removed are marked in red, lines that were added are marked in green, and within a changed line the specific words that differ are highlighted.

It answers a question that is surprisingly hard to settle by reading: "What did they actually change?"

## When do you need to compare two texts?

- **Contracts and agreements.** A rental agreement or vendor contract comes back "with minor edits". A diff shows whether a clause on the security deposit or notice period quietly changed.
- **Assignments and theses.** Students and guides can see what was revised between drafts.
- **Website and app content.** Check that a translated or updated page did not drop a paragraph.
- **Policies and notices.** HR teams can show staff exactly which lines of a leave policy changed.
- **Code and configuration.** Developers compare two versions of a config file or snippet when version control is not available.
- **Data exports.** Compare two lists of GSTINs, roll numbers or product codes to find additions and removals.

## How to compare two texts online

1. Open [Text Compare](https://biscsindia.com/tools/text-diff/).
2. Paste the **Original text** into the left box.
3. Paste the **Changed text** into the right box.
4. The differences appear below straight away, with a summary such as "+3 added, −2 removed, 14 unchanged".
5. Adjust the options: **Ignore whitespace**, **Ignore case**, **Highlight changed words** and **Only show changes**.
6. Use **Swap** if you pasted them the wrong way round.
7. Click **Copy diff** or **Download .diff** to save the result.

Each row shows the line number in the original, the line number in the new version, a plus or minus sign, and the text itself.

## Reading the results

| Colour or symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Green row with + | Line exists only in the changed text (added) |
| Red row with − | Line exists only in the original (removed) |
| Plain row | Line is the same in both |
| Darker highlight inside a row | The exact words that changed in that line |
| Grey bar with ⋯ | Unchanged lines hidden in "Only show changes" mode |

When a line is edited rather than fully replaced, you will see the old version in red directly above the new version in green. With **Highlight changed words** ticked, the tool also compares those two lines word by word, so "delivered in 5 days" next to "delivered in 2 days" highlights just the 5 and the 2.

## Choosing the right options

**Ignore whitespace** is ideal for documents that have been re-typed, copied from PDFs or edited in different apps. Extra spaces and tabs no longer show as changes.

**Ignore case** helps when someone has changed headings from capitals to sentence case and you only care about wording.

**Only show changes** hides long stretches of unchanged text and keeps two lines of context around each change. Turn it on for long contracts so you can jump from edit to edit.

**Highlight changed words** is on by default. Turn it off if you prefer whole lines coloured without inner highlights, for example when comparing lists where each line is a separate item.

## A practical example: checking a rental agreement

Suppose your landlord in Bengaluru emails a revised agreement.

1. Copy the text from the original agreement you signed last year.
2. Copy the text from the new draft. If it is a PDF, extract it with [PDF to Text](https://biscsindia.com/tools/pdf-to-text/).
3. Paste both, tick **Ignore whitespace** and **Only show changes**.
4. Read every green and red row. Look closely at numbers: rent, deposit, notice period, lock-in and maintenance charges.

A diff makes small but important changes, like "two months' notice" becoming "three months' notice", impossible to miss.

## Common mistakes when comparing documents

- **Comparing different line wrapping.** If one copy has a line break every 80 characters and the other has whole paragraphs on one line, everything shows as changed. Clean both first with the [Whitespace Cleaner](https://biscsindia.com/tools/whitespace-cleaner/), using **Remove line breaks** if needed.
- **Pasting in the wrong order.** Additions will show as removals. Use **Swap** to fix it.
- **Assuming formatting is compared.** Bold, italics, colours and fonts are not part of plain text, so a diff will not show them.
- **Ignoring the line numbers.** When discussing changes with someone else, quote the line numbers so you are both looking at the same place.
- **Comparing entirely different texts.** If two texts share almost nothing, a diff is not meaningful, and very large unrelated texts may be too slow to compare.

## Tips for cleaner comparisons

- Sort both lists first with [Sort Lines](https://biscsindia.com/tools/sort-lines/) when order does not matter, so only genuine additions and removals show up.
- Use Find and Replace to normalise things like date formats before comparing data exports.
- For long legal documents, compare section by section if the diff becomes hard to read.
- Save the downloaded `.diff` file alongside the documents as a simple record of what changed and when.

## How does a diff checker decide what changed?

The tool uses a well-known comparison method, the Myers diff algorithm, which is also the basis of many version control systems. It looks for the longest stretch of lines the two texts share and treats everything else as additions or removals, giving the smallest set of edits that turns the original into the new version.

That has a practical side effect. If a paragraph was moved from the top of a document to the bottom, a diff shows it as removed in one place and added in another, rather than "moved". When you see the same text in both red and green, check whether it was simply relocated.

## Are my documents uploaded?

No. [Text Compare](https://biscsindia.com/tools/text-diff/) does the comparison in your browser. Neither version of your text is sent to BISCS India's servers or stored, so it is safe to compare confidential contracts, salary letters or unpublished work. Close the tab and both texts are gone.

Q: Can I compare two Word or PDF files?
A: Copy the text out of each file and paste it into the two boxes. For PDFs, the PDF to Text tool extracts the text first. Formatting such as bold or fonts is not compared, only the words and lines, which is usually what matters when checking a contract or draft.

Q: What does Ignore whitespace do?
A: It treats lines as equal when they differ only in spaces, tabs or extra spacing, for example when one version has double spaces after full stops. This hides noise so you can focus on real wording changes. Turn it off when spacing matters, such as in code or fixed-width data.

Q: Why does a small edit show as a removed line and an added line?
A: The comparison works line by line, so a changed line is shown as the old line removed and the new line added. With Highlight changed words on, the exact words that differ within that pair are marked, so you can still see the small edit at a glance.

Q: Is there a size limit for comparing texts?
A: There is no upload limit because nothing is uploaded, but very large texts that differ almost everywhere can be too slow to compare in a browser. If that happens, the tool tells you, and you can compare the documents in smaller sections.

Q: Can I save the result of the comparison?
A: Yes. Copy diff copies a plain text summary where removed lines start with a minus sign and added lines with a plus sign. Download .diff saves the same summary as a file you can share with a colleague or attach to an email.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- **Pasting Hindi, Bengali or the ₹ symbol.** The standard PDF fonts cannot show them, and they become "?". The tool lists unsupported characters before you create the file; write "Rs." instead of ₹ and keep the text in English.
- **Expecting formatting to carry over.** Bold, italics and bullets from a word processor are lost when copied as plain text. Markdown symbols stay as typed.
- **Using a proportional font for aligned text.** Columns lined up with spaces only stay aligned in Mono.
- **Very small margins.** Many printers cannot print right to the edge. Margins of 15–20 mm print reliably.
- **Very long lines in portrait.** Long log lines wrap and become harder to read. Switch to landscape or reduce the font size.

## Reading Hindi and mixed Hinglish text

Hindi voices read Devanagari text well. Mixed text is trickier:

- A Hindi voice may read English words with a Hindi accent, or spell out unfamiliar ones.
- An Indian English voice will usually skip or mispronounce Devanagari text.
- Hinglish written in Roman script ("aap kaise ho") is read as English and may sound odd.

For best results, match the voice to the main language of the text. If a document mixes both, split it and read each part with the right voice.

## Practical uses

**Proofreading.** Hearing your writing read back is one of the best ways to catch missing words, repeated phrases and clumsy sentences. Your brain skips mistakes when reading silently, but not when listening.

**Learning and revision.** Students can listen to notes while travelling, and language learners can hear how English or Hindi words are pronounced at a slower speed.

**Accessibility.** People with low vision, dyslexia or reading fatigue can listen instead of reading. Older family members can have a WhatsApp forward or a bill read out to them.

**Checking speech timing.** Paste a speech or presentation script, set the speed to match your pace, and see the estimated speaking time. The [Word Counter](https://biscsindia.com/tools/word-counter/) gives a speaking time estimate too.

**Listening to articles.** Copy an article and listen while cooking or commuting. For text inside a PDF, extract it first with [PDF to Text](https://biscsindia.com/tools/pdf-to-text/), or use [Image to Text](https://biscsindia.com/tools/image-to-text/) for a photo or scan.

## Common problems and fixes

- **No sound.** Check that the device is not muted, that the Volume slider is up, and that Bluetooth headphones are connected to the right device.
- **Speech stops part-way.** Some browsers stop when the screen locks or the tab is in the background, especially on phones. Keep the tab open and the screen on.
- **Strange pronunciation of numbers and abbreviations.** Write "Rs" or "rupees" instead of relying on the ₹ symbol, and expand short forms like "approx." if the voice stumbles.
- **Robotic sound.** Try a different voice. Quality varies a lot, and newer voices often sound more natural.
- **Highlighting stays on the whole sentence.** That voice does not report word positions. Choose another voice if you want word-by-word highlighting.

## Tips for better listening

- Clean pasted text first. Broken line breaks from PDFs can cause unnatural pauses, so run it through the [Whitespace Cleaner](https://biscsindia.com/tools/whitespace-cleaner/).
- Use a speed of 1.2× to 1.5× for familiar material and 0.8× for learning or difficult text.
- Add full stops and commas where you want pauses; voices follow punctuation.
- Keep a lower pitch for long sessions, which many people find easier to listen to.

## A quick routine for proofreading by ear

Writers, students and office staff can turn text to speech into a simple editing habit:

1. Finish your draft and paste it into the tool.
2. Choose a clear voice and a speed slightly below normal, around 0.9×.
3. Follow the highlighted words with your eyes while listening.
4. Pause whenever something sounds wrong: a missing "the", a doubled word, a sentence that runs out of breath.
5. Fix the issue in your original document, then carry on.

It works especially well for emails to clients, cover letters and assignment answers, where a single missing word can change the meaning. Ten minutes of listening often catches mistakes that three silent readings missed.

## How to Convert IST to US, UK and Other Time Zones Correctly

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/convert-ist-to-world-time-zones/
Tool: Time Zone Converter (https://biscsindia.com/tools/time-zone-converter/)

Quick answer: India Standard Time is UTC+5:30 all year, with no daylight saving. To convert, find the other city’s current UTC offset and take the difference: 9:00 pm IST is 3:30 pm in London and 10:30 am in New York in November. BISCS India’s free Time Zone Converter shows many world cities at once, adjusting for daylight saving automatically.

India Standard Time (IST) is **UTC+5:30** throughout the year. India does not use daylight saving, so to convert IST to another place you only need that place's current offset from UTC. On a November weekday, **9:00 pm IST is 3:30 pm in London, 7:30 pm in Dubai and 10:30 am in New York**.

The catch is that many countries change their clocks twice a year, so the gap with India shifts. The free [Time Zone Converter](https://biscsindia.com/tools/time-zone-converter/) handles this automatically and shows the time in many cities side by side.

## Why time zone conversion trips people up

- **Daylight saving time (DST).** The US, Canada, UK, most of Europe and parts of Australia move their clocks forward in their summer and back in winter. India does not, so the difference changes by an hour.
- **Different change dates.** The US and Europe switch on different weekends, so for a few weeks a year the usual gaps are off by an hour.
- **Half-hour and quarter-hour offsets.** IST is +5:30 and Nepal is +5:45, which makes mental arithmetic harder.
- **Crossing midnight.** A Monday evening call from India may be Monday morning in the US but already Tuesday in Sydney.

## UTC, GMT and IST: what the labels mean

**UTC** (Coordinated Universal Time) is the world's reference clock. Every time zone is described as an offset from it, such as UTC+5:30 for India or UTC−5 for New York in winter. It never changes for daylight saving.

**GMT** (Greenwich Mean Time) is often used interchangeably with UTC in everyday speech. The UK uses GMT in winter and British Summer Time (BST, UTC+1) in summer, so "London time" and "GMT" are only the same for part of the year.

**IST** is India Standard Time, UTC+5:30, based on a meridian near the centre of the country. All of India, from Gujarat to Arunachal Pradesh, uses this single zone, even though the sun rises much earlier in the north-east than in the west.

Abbreviations can be ambiguous. "IST" is also used for Irish Standard Time and Israel Standard Time, and "CST" can mean China or US Central time. The converter uses full zone names such as *Asia/Kolkata* and *America/Chicago* to avoid this confusion, and you should too in formal communication.

## Worked examples

### A call with a US client

### A morning meeting in Sydney

A Sydney team wants to meet at **9:00 am Tuesday, 10 November 2026**. Sydney is on summer time (UTC+11), so it is **3:30 am Tuesday IST**. An afternoon slot in Sydney works much better for India.

### Family in Dubai

Dubai is UTC+4 all year, so it is always **1 hour 30 minutes behind IST**. A 7:00 pm call in Dubai is 8:30 pm in India.

## Common mistakes when converting time zones

- **Assuming the gap never changes.** It changes for most countries that use daylight saving.
- **Using EST in summer.** New York is on EDT (UTC−4) for most of the year and EST (UTC−5) in winter. Saying "EST" in July is technically wrong and may confuse people.
- **Forgetting the date.** A US Friday evening can already be Saturday morning in India.
- **Ignoring the 30 minutes.** Many quick conversions round IST to +5 or +6 and end up half an hour out.
- **Copying a calendar invite without a time zone.** Always include the zone in invites and emails.

- For recurring meetings, recheck after each daylight saving change.
- Use UTC as a shared reference for global teams.

Q: What is the time difference between India and the USA?
A: It depends on the US time zone and the season, because most of the US uses daylight saving and India does not. New York is 10 hours 30 minutes behind IST in winter and 9 hours 30 minutes behind in summer. Los Angeles is 13 hours 30 minutes behind in winter and 12 hours 30 minutes in summer.

Q: Does India have daylight saving time?
A: No. India uses India Standard Time, UTC+5:30, throughout the year and across the whole country. When other countries move their clocks forward or back, the gap between India and those places changes by an hour, even though Indian clocks stay the same.

Q: Why is IST offset by 30 minutes?
A: India Standard Time is based on the 82.5° E meridian, which runs close to the middle of the country. That longitude corresponds to 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of UTC. Nepal goes further with a 45-minute offset, UTC+5:45, so it is 15 minutes ahead of India.

Q: What happens if I enter a time that does not exist because of daylight saving?
A: When clocks jump forward, an hour is skipped in that zone, for example 2:30 am on the changeover day in New York. The converter detects this, warns you that the local time does not exist, and shows the nearest valid time instead.

Q: Can I add cities that are not in the default list?
A: Yes. Type a city or time zone name such as Europe/Madrid or Auckland in the add box. The converter recognises standard time zone names supported by your browser. Added cities are remembered on your device for your next visit and can be removed at any time.

## Unix Timestamp to Date Converter: Seconds, Milliseconds, IST

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/unix-timestamp-to-date-ist/
Tool: Unix Timestamp Converter (https://biscsindia.com/tools/timestamp-converter/)

Quick answer: A Unix timestamp counts seconds since 1 January 1970 at 00:00 UTC. To read one, convert it to a date in your time zone; for India, that is IST, which is UTC+05:30. BISCS India's Unix Timestamp Converter auto-detects seconds, milliseconds, microseconds and nanoseconds and converts both ways in your browser.

A Unix timestamp, also called epoch time, is simply the number of seconds that have passed since 00:00:00 UTC on 1 January 1970. `1767225600`, for example, is 1 January 2026 at midnight UTC, which is 5:30 am the same day in India.

Computers love timestamps because they are just numbers: easy to store, compare and subtract. People do not, which is why the [Unix Timestamp Converter](https://biscsindia.com/tools/timestamp-converter/) on BISCS India turns them into readable dates in IST, UTC or your device’s zone, and turns dates back into timestamps.

## Why do systems use timestamps instead of dates?

A date like "31/03/2026 10:00" needs context before it means anything: which time zone, which calendar format, whether 03 is the month or the day. A timestamp needs none of that. It identifies one instant, the same everywhere on Earth, as a single integer.

That makes a lot of everyday programming easy. Sorting events is just sorting numbers. Working out how long a delivery took is a subtraction. Checking whether an OTP has expired is a comparison against the current time. And because there is no formatting involved, two systems written in different languages, in different countries, will never disagree about what a timestamp means, only about how to display it.

## Seconds or milliseconds? The most common confusion

Different systems count in different units:

| Unit | Digits today | Example | Typical source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Seconds | 10 | `1767225600` | Unix and Linux, PHP, Python `time.time()` (as a float), JWT `exp`, most APIs |
| Milliseconds | 13 | `1767225600000` | JavaScript `Date.now()`, Java, many JSON APIs |
| Microseconds | 16 | `1767225600000000` | PostgreSQL internals, some logging systems |
| Nanoseconds | 19 | `1767225600000000000` | Go, some databases and tracing tools |

Mixing them up gives absurd results. Treat a millisecond value as seconds and you land tens of thousands of years in the future. Treat seconds as milliseconds and you get a date in January 1970.

In JavaScript, the conversion is one line each way:

```js
const ms = Date.now();                 // 13 digits, milliseconds
const seconds = Math.floor(ms / 1000); // 10 digits, seconds
new Date(seconds * 1000);              // back to a Date
```

## IST is UTC+05:30, all year round

India uses a single time zone, Indian Standard Time, which is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of UTC. There is no daylight saving, so the offset never changes. In time zone databases it is listed as `Asia/Kolkata`.

That half-hour offset catches people out. A server that runs in UTC and writes "18:30" in a log means midnight in India. A report that groups orders "by day" in UTC will put everything placed between midnight and 5:30 am IST into the previous day.

2. Under **Timestamp → date**, paste your timestamp. Commas, underscores and spaces are ignored, so `1,767,225,600` works.
3. Leave **Unit** on **Auto-detect**, or choose seconds, milliseconds, microseconds or nanoseconds yourself.

## Practical examples for Indian developers

- **Reading API responses.** Payment, logistics and messaging APIs often return `created_at` as a timestamp. Paste it in to see exactly when, in IST, an event happened.
- **Debugging JWTs.** The `exp` and `iat` claims are in seconds. The [JWT Decoder](https://biscsindia.com/tools/jwt-decoder/) converts them automatically, but you can also check them here.
- **Scheduling.** If a sale must start at 10:00 am IST on a given date, enter it under Date → timestamp with IST selected and use the resulting UTC-based timestamp in your code or cron configuration.
- **Log analysis.** Server logs in UTC can be matched against customer complaints reported in IST without doing the 5:30 arithmetic in your head.

For converting ordinary meeting times between cities, rather than timestamps, the [Time Zone Converter](https://biscsindia.com/tools/time-zone-converter/) is a better fit.

## ISO 8601: the readable alternative

When you need a human-readable string that is still unambiguous, use ISO 8601 with an offset or a `Z` for UTC:

```text
2026-01-01T00:00:00Z         midnight UTC
2026-01-01T05:30:00+05:30    the same moment, written in IST
```

Both strings describe exactly the same instant. The converter shows the ISO form in UTC, which is what JavaScript’s `toISOString()` produces.

## Common mistakes with timestamps

- **Storing local time without a zone.** A database column holding `2026-03-31 10:00` with no zone is ambiguous. Store a timestamp or UTC, and convert for display.
- **Multiplying or dividing by 1,000 twice.** If dates suddenly appear in 1970 or the far future, check the unit at every step.
- **Using 32-bit integers.** A signed 32-bit seconds counter overflows on 19 January 2038. Use 64-bit integers or your database’s native timestamp type.
- **Assuming the server is in IST.** Most cloud servers default to UTC. Never rely on the machine’s local zone for business logic.
- **Losing precision in JSON.** Nanosecond timestamps have 19 digits, more than JavaScript numbers can hold exactly. Send them as strings.
- **Forgetting leap seconds do not exist here.** Unix time ignores leap seconds, so every day is exactly 86,400 seconds. That makes date arithmetic simple, but do not use it for scientific timekeeping.

## Quick reference

- 1 minute = 60 seconds, 1 hour = 3,600, 1 day = 86,400, 1 week = 604,800.
- IST offset = 19,800 seconds (5.5 × 3,600).
- Timestamp `0` = 1 January 1970, 00:00 UTC = 05:30 IST.
- Negative timestamps represent dates before 1970 and are valid in most modern languages.

If you need the difference between two calendar dates in days, months and years rather than seconds, try the [Date Difference](https://biscsindia.com/tools/date-difference-calculator/) calculator.

## Privacy

All conversions use your browser’s built-in date and `Intl` functions. Nothing you enter is sent anywhere, and the live clock reads your device’s time, so make sure your computer’s clock is set correctly if you rely on the "now" value.

Q: How do I tell if a timestamp is in seconds or milliseconds?
A: Count the digits. Current timestamps in seconds have 10 digits, for example 1767225600. In milliseconds they have 13 digits, like 1767225600000. Microseconds have 16 and nanoseconds 19. The converter’s Auto-detect option uses the digit count, and you can override it if your data is unusual.

Q: Is a Unix timestamp in UTC or local time?
A: A Unix timestamp has no time zone. It is a single count of seconds since the epoch, and the same moment has the same timestamp everywhere in the world. Time zones only matter when you display it as a calendar date, which is where IST, UTC or your local zone comes in.

Q: What is IST in terms of UTC?
A: Indian Standard Time is UTC plus 5 hours 30 minutes, written UTC+05:30. India does not observe daylight saving time, so the offset is the same all year. Midnight UTC is 5:30 am IST, and midnight IST is 6:30 pm UTC on the previous day.

Q: What is the Year 2038 problem?
A: Systems that store Unix time as a signed 32-bit integer can only count up to 19 January 2038 at 03:14:07 UTC. After that the value overflows. Modern operating systems, databases and languages mostly use 64-bit time, but old embedded devices and legacy code may still be affected.

Q: Why is my converted date 5 hours 30 minutes off?
A: Somewhere a time was treated as UTC when it was really IST, or the other way round. Common causes are saving a local IST time without zone information and later reading it as UTC, or a server set to UTC formatting dates for Indian users. Store timestamps or UTC, and convert only for display.

## Common conversion mistakes

- **Converting area with a length factor.** 1 m is 3.28 ft, but 1 sq m is 10.76 sq ft, because you square the factor.
- **Mixing US and UK units,** especially gallons, pints and fluid ounces.
- **Assuming a bigha is the same everywhere.** It is not.
- **Rounding too early.** Keep extra decimals until the final answer, especially for land and gold, where small differences cost money.
- **Adding 32 before multiplying** when converting Celsius to Fahrenheit. Multiply first, then add.
- **Confusing GB and GiB** when checking storage or download sizes.

## Metric and imperial: why India uses both

India adopted the metric system officially decades ago, and science, trade and government records use it. Yet older units survive in daily speech. People quote height in feet and inches, TV and phone screens in inches, flats in square feet, and land in acres, cents, guntha or bigha depending on the region.

At the same time, many online recipes, product listings and fitness apps come from the US or UK, where pounds, ounces, cups and miles are common. A converter that holds both systems side by side, with the Indian units added, saves you from searching for a different factor every time.

Q: How many square feet are in one acre, cent and guntha?
A: One acre is 43,560 square feet. One cent is one hundredth of an acre, or 435.6 square feet, and one guntha is one fortieth of an acre, or 1,089 square feet. A square yard, often called a gaj, is 9 square feet.

Q: Why does my 1 TB hard drive show only about 931 GB?

Q: Is a US gallon the same as a UK gallon?

Q: How much is one tola of gold in grams?

## URL Encode and Decode: Percent-Encoding Explained Simply

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/url-encode-decode-percent-encoding/
Tool: URL Encode / Decode (https://biscsindia.com/tools/url-encoder/)

Quick answer: URL encoding, or percent-encoding, replaces characters that are unsafe in a web address with a % sign and their byte value in hex, so a space becomes %20 and & becomes %26. BISCS India's URL Encode / Decode tool converts both ways, supports component and full-URL modes, and breaks any URL into its parts in your browser.

URL encoding, properly called percent-encoding, is how web addresses carry characters that would otherwise break them. A space becomes `%20`, an ampersand becomes `%26`, and the rupee sign becomes `%E2%82%B9`. Each `%XX` is one byte written in hexadecimal.

You need it whenever you put user text, search terms or another URL inside a link. The [URL Encode / Decode](https://biscsindia.com/tools/url-encoder/) tool on BISCS India converts both ways, lets you choose between component and full-URL encoding, and includes a URL parser that splits any address into its parts.

## Why do URLs need encoding at all?

A URL has structure. The `?` starts the query string, `&` separates parameters, `=` joins a key to its value, `#` starts a fragment and `/` separates path segments. If your data contains any of these characters, the browser and server cannot tell data from structure.

Imagine a search for "salt & pepper" on a shopping site:

```text
https://shop.example.com/search?q=salt & pepper&sort=price
```

The server sees a parameter `q` with value `salt `, then a broken parameter called ` pepper`. Encoded properly, it is unambiguous:

```text
https://shop.example.com/search?q=salt%20%26%20pepper&sort=price
```

## encodeURIComponent vs encodeURI

JavaScript has two built-in functions, and the tool offers both under **Type**.

| Function | Leaves alone | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `encodeURIComponent` | Letters, digits and `- _ . ! ~ * ' ( )` | One parameter value, a path segment, a URL inside another URL |
| `encodeURI` | All of the above plus `; , / ? : @ & = + $ #` | A whole URL that is already correctly built |

The rule of thumb: encode each **piece** with `encodeURIComponent`, then join the pieces. Using `encodeURI` on a parameter value is a classic bug, because it leaves `&` and `=` unencoded.

```js
const city = 'Mumbai & Thane';
const url = 'https://api.example.com/stores?city=' + encodeURIComponent(city);
// https://api.example.com/stores?city=Mumbai%20%26%20Thane
```

For building URLs in code, the `URLSearchParams` object handles this for you and is usually the cleanest option.

## How to encode or decode a URL with BISCS India

1. Open [URL Encode / Decode](https://biscsindia.com/tools/url-encoder/).
2. Choose **Encode** or **Decode**.
3. Select the **Type**: **Component (encodeURIComponent)** for a single value, or **Full URL (encodeURI)** for a whole address.
4. Tick **Spaces as + (form encoding)** if you are working with HTML form data.
5. Paste your text or URL into **Input**. The **Output** updates as you type.
6. Click **Copy**, or **Swap** to move the output back into the input and reverse the direction.

If decoding fails, for example because of a stray `%` not followed by two hex digits, the tool tells you instead of returning half-decoded text.

If you build campaign links regularly, the [UTM Link Builder](https://biscsindia.com/tools/utm-builder/) creates correctly encoded tracking URLs from a simple form.

## Which characters are safe in a URL without encoding?

The URL standard defines a small set of "unreserved" characters that never need encoding: the letters `A–Z` and `a–z`, the digits `0–9`, and four symbols, hyphen, full stop, underscore and tilde. Everything else either has a structural job (the reserved characters such as `/ ? # & =`) or is simply not allowed, like spaces, quotation marks, angle brackets and any non-ASCII character.

That is why a well-chosen slug such as `/blog/gst-invoice-format` travels everywhere untouched, while a path like `/files/Annual Report 2025.pdf` has to become `/files/Annual%20Report%202025.pdf`. If you control the names of pages and files, sticking to lowercase letters, digits and hyphens avoids encoding problems entirely.

## How do other languages encode URLs?

Most programming languages have an equivalent of `encodeURIComponent`, but the defaults differ slightly, which is a common source of mismatched signatures and broken API calls:

- **Python:** `urllib.parse.quote(value, safe='')` encodes a component; `urllib.parse.urlencode()` builds a whole query string and uses `+` for spaces.
- **PHP:** `rawurlencode()` follows the standard with `%20` for spaces, while `urlencode()` uses `+`, form-style.
- **Java:** `URLEncoder.encode(value, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)` is designed for form data, so it also turns spaces into `+`.

When two systems disagree on a value, paste both versions into the decoder. If one shows `+` and the other `%20`, you have found the difference, and you can tick or untick **Spaces as +** to match the system you are talking to.

## What happens to Indian-language text?

URLs travel as ASCII. Non-ASCII text is first converted to UTF-8 bytes, and each byte is percent-encoded. Devanagari, Bengali and Tamil characters use three bytes each, so a short Hindi word turns into a long string of `%E0%A4…` codes.

Modern browsers display the readable form in the address bar, but copy-paste often gives you the encoded form. The decoder turns it back. For website page addresses, plain English slugs are usually easier to share; the [Slug Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/slug-generator/) can create one from any title.

## Common mistakes with URL encoding

- **Double encoding.** Encoding an already-encoded string turns `%20` into `%2520`. If a server shows `%20` literally on the page, something encoded twice.
- **Encoding the whole URL with encodeURIComponent.** This turns `https://` into `https%3A%2F%2F` and the link stops working. Only use component encoding on pieces.
- **Forgetting to encode user input.** A customer name like `D'Souza & Sons` will break a query string if inserted raw.
- **Mixing up + and %20.** In a path, `+` is a literal plus. In form-encoded query strings, it means space. Know which context you are in.
- **Confusing URL encoding with Base64.** They solve different problems. For binary data in a URL, use URL-safe Base64 from the [Base64 Encode / Decode](https://biscsindia.com/tools/base64-encoder/) tool.

## Privacy

Links frequently contain session tokens, email addresses or reset codes in their query strings. The encoder and the parser run entirely in your browser using the standard `encodeURIComponent`, `decodeURIComponent` and `URL` functions, so nothing you paste is uploaded or logged.

Q: What does %20 mean in a URL?
A: %20 is the percent-encoded form of a space character. Spaces are not allowed in URLs, so they are replaced by a percent sign followed by the character’s hexadecimal byte value, which is 20 for a space. In HTML form submissions, a space may instead appear as a plus sign.

Q: Should I use encodeURI or encodeURIComponent?
A: Use encodeURIComponent for a single piece of a URL, such as one query parameter value or a path segment, because it also encodes reserved characters like &, = and /. Use encodeURI only for a complete URL that is already correctly structured, since it leaves those structural characters alone.

Q: Why do I see a + instead of a space in some URLs?
A: HTML forms submitted with the application/x-www-form-urlencoded format encode spaces as + rather than %20. Both are common in query strings. When decoding form data, tick the Spaces as + option so that plus signs are turned back into spaces instead of being kept as literal plus characters.

Q: Why is my Hindi text in a URL shown as lots of % codes?
A: Non-ASCII characters are first converted to UTF-8 bytes, and each byte is then percent-encoded. A single Devanagari letter takes three bytes in UTF-8, so it becomes three %XX groups. Browsers often display the readable version in the address bar but send the encoded form.

Q: Can URL encoding break a link if done twice?
A: Yes. Encoding an already-encoded URL turns each % into %25, so %20 becomes %2520 and the server receives the wrong text. If you see %25 in a link, it has probably been double-encoded. Decode it once and check that the result looks right.

A UTM link is your normal web address with a few extra tags at the end, like `?utm_source=whatsapp&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=diwali_sale`. When someone clicks it, Google Analytics reads those tags and records exactly which campaign sent them.

## Why tag links at all?

Without tags, much of your marketing traffic lands in vague buckets. Visits from WhatsApp forwards, email newsletters, PDF brochures and many mobile apps often show up as "direct" because no referrer is passed. You cannot tell whether the Diwali offer you broadcast to customers worked better than the Instagram story.

UTM tags fix that. Each tagged link carries its own label, so your analytics can show sessions, enquiries and sales per campaign.

## What each UTM parameter means

| Parameter | Answers | Example values |
|---|---|---|
| `utm_source` | Where did the visitor come from? | whatsapp, newsletter, google, facebook |

Source, medium and campaign are the core three. Google Analytics relies on source and medium to place traffic into channel groups such as Email, Organic Social or Paid Search, so consistent medium values make your reports far more useful.

## A naming convention that keeps reports clean

The biggest UTM problem is inconsistency. One person writes "WhatsApp", another "whatsapp", a third "wa", and your report now has three sources for one channel. Agree a short convention and write it down:

- **Lowercase everything.** The builder does this by default.
- **Use underscores instead of spaces.** `summer_sale`, not `summer sale` (which becomes `summer%20sale`).
- **Fix your medium list.** For example: `social`, `email`, `cpc`, `qr`, `sms`, `referral`. Do not invent new ones per campaign.
- **Name campaigns by what and when.** `ipl_offer_apr`, `gst_webinar_nov`.
- **Use utm_content for variations.** If one email has a button and a text link, tag them `button` and `text_link` to see which gets clicked.

## Practical examples for Indian businesses

**A CA firm's monthly newsletter:** source `newsletter`, medium `email`, campaign `itr_deadline_reminder`. Any reader who clicks through to the ITR filing page is recorded under that campaign.

**A printed brochure at a trade fair:** source `brochure`, medium `qr`, campaign `pragati_maidan_expo`. Print the QR code from the builder so visits from the fair stand out.

## Common UTM mistakes

- **Tagging internal links.** Using UTM links in your own menu or between your own pages overwrites the original source and corrupts your data. Only tag links that point to your site from elsewhere.
- **Skipping the medium.** Without it, channel reports group visits poorly. The builder warns when it is missing.
- **Mixing cases.** "Facebook" and "facebook" become two sources.
- **Breaking single-page app URLs.** Some sites put a `?` after the `#`. The builder places tags before the `#`, where analytics tools can read them, and warns you.
- **Sharing ugly links.** Long tagged URLs look suspicious in a chat. Put them behind a button, a QR code or descriptive link text where possible.

- **Key events.** If you have set up events for form submissions, calls or purchases, add them as a column to see which campaigns produce real enquiries, not just visits.
- **Explorations.** For deeper analysis, build a free-form exploration with source, medium, campaign and content as rows.

Give a campaign a week or two before drawing conclusions, especially for small businesses with modest traffic. A handful of visits is not enough to judge one channel against another.

## UUID Generator: UUID v4 vs v7 and When to Use Each

URL: https://biscsindia.com/blog/uuid-v4-vs-v7-generator/
Tool: UUID Generator (https://biscsindia.com/tools/uuid-generator/)

Quick answer: A UUID is a 128-bit identifier written as 36 characters, such as 3f2b8c1e-9a4d-4f6b-8e2a-1c7d5e9f0a3b, that can be created anywhere without a central counter. Use v4 for purely random IDs and v7 when you want IDs that sort by creation time. BISCS India's UUID Generator creates up to 1,000 of either, securely, in your browser.

A UUID (universally unique identifier) is a 128-bit label that you can generate on any computer, at any time, without checking with a central database, and still be confident nobody else will ever produce the same one. It looks like this:

```text
6f1c2a9e-3b7d-4c58-9e21-0a4f7b3d5c86
```

The [UUID Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/uuid-generator/) on BISCS India creates version 4 (random) or version 7 (time-ordered) UUIDs, from one to a thousand at a time, using your browser’s cryptographically secure random number generator. It can also tell you the version of any UUID you paste in.

## Why use UUIDs instead of 1, 2, 3?

Auto-incrementing numbers are simple, but they have drawbacks once a system grows:

- **They need one source of truth.** Two servers, a mobile app working offline, or two merged databases cannot safely invent the next number on their own.
- **They leak information.** An invoice URL ending `/orders/10452` tells a competitor roughly how many orders you have taken, and invites people to try `/orders/10453`.
- **They collide when data is combined.** Merging records from two branches, both starting at 1, needs renumbering.

UUIDs solve all three. Any device can mint its own, and they will not clash.

## Reading a UUID

A UUID is 32 hexadecimal digits split into groups of 8-4-4-4-12. Two positions carry metadata:

```text
6f1c2a9e-3b7d-4c58-9e21-0a4f7b3d5c86
              ^    ^
              |    variant (8, 9, a or b for standard UUIDs)
              version (4 here)
```

The first digit of the third group is the **version**. The first digit of the fourth group shows the **variant**, which for every modern UUID is 8, 9, a or b.

## UUID v4 vs UUID v7

| | Version 4 | Version 7 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contents | 122 random bits | 48-bit Unix timestamp (ms) + random bits |
| Sorts by creation time | No | Yes |
| Reveals creation time | No | Yes |
| Database index friendliness | Poor at large scale | Good |
| Standard | RFC 4122, now RFC 9562 | RFC 9562 (2024) |
| Best for | Public IDs, tokens, general use | Primary keys, logs, event IDs |

**Version 4** is the long-standing default. Every bit apart from the version and variant is random, so v4 UUIDs reveal nothing and are scattered evenly.

**Version 7** was standardised in 2024. It starts with the current time in milliseconds, then fills the rest with random bits. As a result, v7 UUIDs generated later sort after those generated earlier. This tool also keeps UUIDs created within the same millisecond in order, using a small counter.

### Why ordering matters for databases

Most databases store primary keys in a B-tree index. Random v4 keys land at random positions, so the database keeps splitting and rewriting index pages, which slows inserts and bloats storage once tables reach millions of rows. Time-ordered v7 keys always go at the end, much like an auto-increment number, while keeping the benefits of a UUID.

If you are starting a new table in PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQL Server and want UUID keys, v7 is generally the better pick.

## What about UUID v1 and other versions?

You may come across other versions in older systems. **Version 1** combines a timestamp with the machine’s network card (MAC) address, which leaks hardware details and is rarely recommended today. **Versions 3 and 5** are not random at all: they are created by hashing a namespace and a name, so the same input always gives the same UUID, which is useful when you need a stable ID for something like a URL. **Version 6** is a reordered v1 designed to sort by time, but v7 achieves the same goal more simply.

For almost all new work, the choice comes down to v4 or v7, which is why this tool focuses on those two. Its validator still recognises the version number of any standard UUID you paste, so you can identify IDs coming from older code.

2. Under **Version**, pick **v4 (random)** or **v7 (time-ordered)**.
3. Enter **How many** you need, from 1 to 1,000.

The **Quotes + commas** option is handy for seeding test data. For example, ten v4 UUIDs ready for a JavaScript array:

```js
  "0c8e4b1f-7d2a-4e93-b6f1-5a3c9d2e7f80",
  "a41f9c3e-2b6d-4f07-8c15-e9d3b7a2c614",
  // ...
];
```

## Checking an existing UUID

Paste any UUID into **Validate a UUID**. The tool accepts it with or without hyphens, braces, quotes or a `urn:uuid:` prefix, and tells you whether it is valid and which version it is. For a v7 UUID, it also decodes the embedded timestamp and shows the creation time in IST.

This is useful when you are debugging and want to know whether an ID came from your new v7 code path or an older v4 one, or roughly when a record was created.

## Generating UUIDs in code

You rarely need a library any more. Modern browsers and Node.js have a built-in v4 generator:

```js
crypto.randomUUID();   // e.g. "36b8f84d-df4e-4d49-b662-bcde71a8764f"
```

Python offers `uuid.uuid4()`, and PostgreSQL has `gen_random_uuid()`. Support for v7 is newer and varies, so check your language or database version, or generate v7 values with a maintained library.

## Common mistakes with UUIDs

- **Using `Math.random()` to build UUIDs.** It is not cryptographically secure and can produce collisions in some environments. Use `crypto.randomUUID()` or `crypto.getRandomValues()`.
- **Storing UUIDs as 36-character strings in large tables.** Where available, use a native UUID or 16-byte binary column type, which is smaller and faster to index.
- **Treating UUIDs as secrets.** They are designed to be unique, not unguessable. Use dedicated random tokens for password resets and API keys; the [Password Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/password-generator/) can produce long random strings for manual use.
- **Exposing v7 IDs where timing is sensitive.** Anyone can read the timestamp.
- **Mixing formats.** Uppercase, braces and no-hyphen forms represent the same value, but string comparisons will treat them as different. Normalise to lowercase with hyphens.

## Privacy and randomness

Every UUID is generated in your browser with `crypto.randomUUID()` or `crypto.getRandomValues()`, the same secure random source browsers use for encryption keys. Nothing is requested from a server and nothing is stored. For other kinds of random values, such as lottery-style draws, try the [Random Number Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/random-number-generator/), and for fingerprints of data rather than identifiers, the [Hash Generator](https://biscsindia.com/tools/hash-generator/).

Q: What is the difference between a UUID and a GUID?
A: They are the same thing. GUID, short for globally unique identifier, is the name Microsoft uses, while UUID is the name in the formal standard. Both are 128-bit values written as 32 hexadecimal digits in five hyphen-separated groups. Some Microsoft tools display GUIDs in uppercase or inside curly braces.

Q: Can two random UUIDs ever be the same?
A: In theory yes, in practice no. A version 4 UUID has 122 random bits. You would need to generate billions of UUIDs every second for many decades before a single duplicate became likely, provided they come from a cryptographically secure random generator, as they do in this tool.

Q: Should I use UUID v4 or v7 as a database primary key?
A: UUID v7 is usually the better choice for primary keys. Because it begins with a timestamp, new rows are inserted at the end of the index instead of at random positions, which keeps B-tree indexes compact and inserts fast. Use v4 when you do not want the creation time to be visible.

Q: Does a UUID v7 reveal when it was created?
A: Yes. The first 48 bits are the Unix timestamp in milliseconds, so anyone can read the creation time. The validator in this tool shows it in IST. If creation time is sensitive, for example in public URLs where it could reveal activity patterns, use a v4 UUID instead.

Q: Are UUIDs safe to use as secret tokens?
A: A v4 UUID from a secure generator is hard to guess, but UUIDs were designed to be unique, not secret. For password reset links, API keys or session tokens, prefer a purpose-built random token of at least 128 bits from your framework, and never use v1 or v7 UUIDs, which contain predictable time information.

To compress a video, you re-encode it so it uses fewer bits per second: with a more efficient codec, a lower resolution, a lower bitrate, or all three. A 120 MB clip from a modern phone can often become 15–30 MB and still look good on a phone screen.

The [Video Compressor](https://biscsindia.com/tools/video-compressor/) on BISCS India does this in your browser. ## Why are phone videos so large?

Phones record at high resolution (1080p or 4K) and high bitrates so the footage looks great and can be edited later. A single minute of 4K video can easily run into hundreds of megabytes.

That is far more than you need to watch a clip on a phone, but it collides with real-world limits:

- **WhatsApp** has commonly capped normal video messages at around 16 MB at the time of writing; check the app, as limits change.
- **Email** services commonly allow attachments of around 20–25 MB, with Gmail typically at 25 MB at the time of writing. Larger files are often turned into cloud links.
- **Government portals, job sites and college admission forms** often set their own upload limits, such as 10 MB or 50 MB. The form usually states it next to the upload button.

## Key terms in plain English

- **Resolution** is the picture size in pixels: 1080p is 1920 × 1080, 720p is 1280 × 720, 480p is about 854 × 480. Halving the height roughly quarters the number of pixels to store.
- **Bitrate** is how much data is used per second of video, measured in kilobits per second (kbps). File size is roughly bitrate × duration.
- **Codec** is the method used to compress the pictures. This tool encodes to **H.264** video with **AAC** audio, the combination nearly every phone, browser, TV and app can play.
- **Container** is the file wrapper, here **MP4**.

3. Pick a preset:
   - **WhatsApp:** aims for 16 MB or less at 720p.

## Which preset should you choose?

| Goal | Preset | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Send a clip on WhatsApp | WhatsApp | 720p |
| Attach to an email | Email | 720p |
| Upload to a form with a fixed limit | Target size | 720p, or 480p for long videos |

A useful rule: if a target size is very small for the length of the video, **lower the resolution**. A clean 480p video looks much better than a blocky, smeared 1080p one squeezed into the same size. The tool warns you when the bitrate it has to use is very low.

## How target size works

When you set a target size, the compressor works out a bitrate from the size and the duration of the video, reserves a little for audio and container overhead, and encodes to that bitrate. For example, 16 MB for a 60-second clip leaves roughly 2 megabits per second in total, which is comfortable for 720p. The same 16 MB for a 10-minute video leaves only about 200 kbps, which is why longer videos need a lower resolution to stay watchable.

## Tips for better results

- **Trim first.** Cutting the unneeded start and end with the [Video Trimmer](https://biscsindia.com/tools/video-trimmer/) is the easiest way to save space.
- **Remove audio from silent clips.** Screen recordings or product demos without narration do not need an audio track.
- **Avoid compressing the same video repeatedly.** Each re-encode loses a little more quality. Always compress from the original.
- **Use a computer for long or 4K videos.** Phones can do it, but large files are processed in memory and may fail on devices with little RAM. The tool warns you when a file is large.
- **Keep the tab open.** Switching away on some phones can pause or stop the processing.

## Common mistakes

- **Expecting miracles from already-compressed files.** Videos downloaded from social media or forwarded on chat apps are already small. Recompressing them gains little and loses quality.
- **Choosing 1080p for a tiny target.** As explained above, resolution must suit the bitrate.
- **Renaming the file extension instead of converting.** Changing `.mov` to `.mp4` does not change the codec inside. Use the compressor or the [Video Converter & MP3](https://biscsindia.com/tools/video-converter/).
- **Forgetting that WhatsApp may compress again.** Even after you hit the limit, the app may re-compress on sending. Sending as a document avoids that, if the recipient does not need an inline preview.

## Containers and codecs, explained simply

Video files confuse people because two separate things are going on, and file names show only one of them.

- **The container** is the box: MP4, MOV, MKV, WebM. It is what the extension tells you. A container holds a video track, one or more audio tracks and some information such as duration.
- **The codec** is how the contents of the box were compressed: H.264, HEVC (H.265), VP9 or AV1 for video; AAC, MP3 or Opus for audio.

A device needs to understand both. A `.mp4` file can still fail to play if the video inside uses a codec the device does not support. That is why simply renaming `video.mov` to `video.mp4` does not work: the box gets a new label, but the contents are unchanged.

## Which format should you choose?

| Format | Inside (this tool) | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MP4 | H.264 + AAC | Sharing anywhere: WhatsApp, phones, PowerPoint, TVs |
| WebM | VP8/VP9 + Opus | Web pages, open formats |
| MOV | H.264 + AAC | Apple apps and some editing workflows |
| MKV | H.264 + AAC | Archiving, media players such as VLC |
| MP3 | Audio only | Universal audio: phones, car stereos, podcasts |
| M4A | AAC audio | Apple devices, good quality at small sizes |
| WAV | Uncompressed audio | Editing in audio software; large files |

If you are unsure, choose **MP4** for video and **MP3** for audio. They work almost everywhere.

## Extracting audio: MP3 from a video

Choosing MP3, M4A or WAV for a video file keeps only the sound. Common reasons include:

- Saving a recorded lecture or seminar to listen to on a commute.
- Getting the audio of a family function video to share with elderly relatives on a basic phone.
- Pulling a voice-over out of a screen recording to edit it separately.
- Turning a recorded song practice into an audio file for your teacher.

As a guide, 128 kbps MP3 is fine for speech, while 192 kbps or more suits music. WAV is uncompressed, about 10 MB per minute, so use it only if you will edit the audio further. For recording new audio directly, or trimming an existing clip before export, the [Audio Recorder & Converter](https://biscsindia.com/tools/audio-recorder/) is a better fit.

## Speed: copying vs re-encoding

**Stream copy** moves the existing video and audio into a new container without touching them. Converting an iPhone MOV that already contains H.264 to MP4 this way takes seconds and loses nothing.

**Re-encoding** decodes every frame and compresses it again. It is needed when the codec must change, for example HEVC to H.264, or any conversion to WebM. It takes longer and depends heavily on your device: a laptop is much faster than a phone, and long or 4K videos can take many minutes. The converter tries a copy first when the option is ticked and falls back to re-encoding automatically when needed.

## Tips and common mistakes

- **Do not rename extensions to convert.** Use a converter so the codec actually changes.
- **Do not convert repeatedly.** Each re-encode loses a little quality. Always convert from the original file.
- **Keep the resolution at Original** unless you also want a smaller file. Lowering it forces a re-encode. If size is your real goal, the [Video Compressor](https://biscsindia.com/tools/video-compressor/) has presets for WhatsApp, email and exact sizes.
- **Expect larger WAV files.** That is normal, not a fault.
- **Keep the tab open** during long conversions, especially on phones, where switching apps can pause the browser.
- **Trim first if you only need part of it.** The [Video Trimmer](https://biscsindia.com/tools/video-trimmer/) cuts without re-encoding, and a shorter clip converts faster.

## Privacy and limits

The conversion runs on your own device using a browser build of the FFmpeg engine, the same open-source engine many desktop apps use behind the scenes. Your video is never uploaded, so personal and work recordings stay private. Very large files are processed in memory, which can fail on phones or older computers; the tool warns you before starting if a file is large, and a shorter clip is the easiest workaround.

Q: What is the best video format for sharing?
A: MP4 with H.264 video and AAC audio is the safest choice. It plays on Android phones, iPhones, Windows and Mac computers, smart TVs, WhatsApp, PowerPoint and almost every website. Use WebM mainly for web pages, and MOV when an Apple editing workflow specifically asks for it.

Q: Why won’t my MOV file from an iPhone play on Windows or Android?
A: Newer iPhones often record in HEVC, also called H.265, inside a MOV file. Some Windows PCs, older Android phones and websites cannot decode HEVC without extra support. Converting to MP4 with H.264 solves this. Note that HEVC files may also fail to preview in some browsers, though the converter can usually still read them.

Q: Which audio bitrate should I choose for MP3?
A: For speech such as lectures, interviews or voice notes, 128 kbps is plenty. For music, 192 kbps sounds good to most listeners, and 320 kbps is the highest common MP3 setting. A higher bitrate cannot restore quality the original video never had, so do not exceed the source quality.

Q: Is it legal to extract audio from a YouTube or film video?
A: The tool converts files already on your device; it does not download from websites. Whether you may use the audio depends on copyright and the platform’s terms. Your own recordings, licensed material and content whose owner gave permission are fine. Commercial films and songs generally are not yours to redistribute.

Q: What does Copy streams when possible do?
A: If the video and audio inside your file already use codecs the new container supports, the converter copies them into the new wrapper without re-encoding. That is much faster and loses no quality. If the codecs are not compatible, it automatically re-encodes instead. This option is not available for WebM output or when changing resolution.

## Why GIFs need special care

GIF is an old format. Each frame can use at most 256 colours, and its compression is primitive compared with modern video codecs such as H.264. That causes two familiar problems:

- **Big files.** A five-second clip at full HD can run to tens of megabytes as a GIF.
- **Banding and speckles.** Skies, skin tones and gradients have more than 256 shades, so they look stepped or grainy.

Good GIF makers fight both. This tool uses a two-pass process: first it analyses your clip and builds the best 256-colour palette for it, then it renders every frame using that palette with your chosen dithering. That gives noticeably better colours than a generic palette.

## How to make a GIF with BISCS India

2. Choose a video or drag it in. MP4, MOV, WebM, MKV and AVI files are supported.
3. Drag the handles over the thumbnail strip to select the part you want. Keep it short: two to six seconds is ideal.
4. In **GIF settings**, set **Frames per second** (5 to 25, default 12) and **Width** (240 to 800 px). The height follows automatically to keep the shape.
5. Choose **Dithering**: **Smooth** for nicer gradients or **Compact** for smaller files.
6. Leave **Loop forever** ticked for a classic GIF, or untick it to play once.
7. Click **Make GIF**. The first time, a video engine of about 32 MB downloads once and is cached by your browser.
8. Preview the result with its size, dimensions and length, then download it. If the GIF is large, click **Make MP4 instead (smaller)** for a lightweight silent video of the same clip.

## Settings that control file size

GIF size grows with every setting, roughly multiplying together:

| Setting | Effect on size | Suggested value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Length | Doubles when the clip doubles | 2–6 seconds |
| Frames per second | More frames, more data | 10–15 fps |
| Width | Height scales too, so pixels grow fast | 320–480 px for chat, up to 800 for docs |
| Dithering | Compact is usually smaller | Smooth for photos, Compact for screen recordings |
| Content | Busy, moving backgrounds compress poorly | Steady camera, simple backgrounds |

If a GIF is over a size limit, cut the length first, then reduce the width, then the frame rate. The tool warns you when a GIF comes out larger than about 8 MB.

## GIF or MP4? Choose by where it is going

Many platforms that seem to show GIFs are actually playing short silent videos, because video is so much more efficient. The tool’s MP4 option makes the same clip at the same width and frame rate, usually five to ten times smaller than the GIF, and most chat apps such as WhatsApp and Telegram loop it like a GIF.

Use a **GIF** when:

- The destination accepts images but not video, such as many email newsletters, GitHub README files, wikis and older forums.
- You want it to play everywhere automatically without any player controls.

Use the **MP4** when:

- You are posting to chat apps or social media that accept video.
- File size matters, for example on a website where page speed counts.

## Tips for better-looking GIFs

- **Trim tightly.** The best GIFs show one action, starting and ending at natural moments. If the loop point jumps, try shifting the end slightly.
- **Use a steady shot.** Camera shake changes every pixel on every frame, which bloats the file. Screen recordings and tripod shots make excellent GIFs.
- **Go narrow for chat.** 320–480 px wide looks fine on a phone and keeps the file small.
- **Choose Compact for screen recordings.** Interfaces have flat colours, so the ordered pattern is barely visible and saves space.
- **Choose Smooth for real-world footage.** Faces, food and landscapes benefit from gentler dithering.
- **Record specially for a GIF.** For a software demo, capture just the window you need with the [Screen Recorder](https://biscsindia.com/tools/screen-recorder/), then convert a few seconds of it.

## Common mistakes

- **Converting a whole video.** A one-minute GIF is almost always too large to be useful. Cut out the essential moment, or use the [Video Trimmer](https://biscsindia.com/tools/video-trimmer/) for a longer clip you share as video instead.
- **Using maximum width and frame rate.** 800 px at 25 fps looks nice but produces huge files. Increase settings only if the default looks poor.
- **Expecting sound.** GIFs are always silent.
- **Uploading a giant GIF to a website.** Large GIFs slow pages down. Consider the MP4, or compress other heavy media with the [Video Compressor](https://biscsindia.com/tools/video-compressor/).

## Privacy and performance

The GIF is created on your device using a browser build of the FFmpeg engine; your video is not uploaded anywhere. Because your own processor does the work, a computer is faster than a phone, and very large source videos can fail on devices with little memory. Selecting a short clip keeps processing quick on any device.

Q: Why are GIF files so large?
A: GIF is a format from the late 1980s. It stores up to 256 colours per frame and uses compression that is far less efficient than modern video codecs. A few seconds of smooth motion can easily reach several megabytes. Keeping clips short, narrow and at 10 to 15 frames per second keeps sizes reasonable.

Q: What is the best frame rate for a GIF?
A: Around 10 to 15 frames per second suits most GIFs. It looks smooth enough for reactions, screen demos and product loops while keeping the file small. Use higher rates, up to 25, only for fast action that looks jerky otherwise, and accept that the file will grow noticeably.

Q: Do GIFs have sound?
A: No. The GIF format cannot contain audio, so any sound in your video is dropped. If you need sound, share the trimmed clip as an MP4 instead. The optional MP4 version this tool creates is also silent, because it is meant as a lightweight GIF replacement.

Q: Should I use a GIF or a short MP4?
A: A short silent MP4 is usually five to ten times smaller than the same GIF and looks better, and many chat apps and websites loop it just like a GIF. Use a GIF where video is not accepted, such as some email clients, documentation tools, forums and older platforms.

Q: What does the Smooth or Compact dithering option change?
A: Dithering mixes dots of the limited palette colours to imitate shades the GIF cannot store. Smooth uses error-diffusion dithering, which gives gentler gradients but slightly larger files. Compact uses a regular ordered pattern that compresses better, at the cost of a visible fine texture in gradients.

## When is trimming useful?

- Removing dead time from the start and end of a phone video before sharing it in a family WhatsApp group.
- Cutting a short clip of a child’s school performance from a long recording.
- Extracting one answer from a recorded webinar or online class to send to a colleague.
- Shortening a product demo to fit a platform’s duration limit, such as for a story or reel.
- Cleaning up a screen recording before sending it to a client.

## Fast vs Precise: how video cutting really works

To understand the two modes, it helps to know how video is stored. Compressed video does not save every frame as a full picture. It saves a complete image, called a **keyframe**, every so often, often every one to a few seconds, and in between it stores only what changed.

That leads to a trade-off:

| | Fast | Precise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Re-encodes the video | No (stream copy) | Yes |
| Speed | Seconds, even for long files | Slower; depends on clip length and device |
| Quality | Identical to original | Very slightly reduced, usually invisible |
| Cut accuracy | Starts at the nearest keyframe, can be a few seconds early | Exact frame |
| Output format | Same as the original where possible | MP4 (or WebM for WebM sources) |

**Use Fast** for everyday trimming, where a second or two of extra footage at the start does not matter. **Use Precise** when the clip must start on an exact moment, such as the first word of a sentence or the start of a goal.

4. For more control, play the video and use **Set start here** and **Set end here** at the current playhead, or type exact times such as `1:23.5` or `83.5`.

## Tips for clean cuts

- **Keep the original.** Trimming creates a new file; your original stays untouched on your device. Keep it until you are sure the clip is right.
- **Use the keyboard for fine tuning.** The start and end controls are sliders, so on a computer you can focus a handle and use the arrow keys for small adjustments.

## Common mistakes

- **Trimming a huge 4K file on an old phone.** The browser holds the file in memory, which can fail on devices with little RAM. A computer handles big files far better, and the tool warns you when a file is large.

Q: Does trimming a video reduce its quality?
A: Not in Fast mode. It copies the original video and audio data without re-encoding, so the kept part is bit-for-bit the same quality. Precise mode re-encodes the clip to cut on an exact frame, which involves a small, usually invisible, quality trade-off and takes longer.

Q: Why does my Fast-mode clip start a little earlier than I selected?
A: Compressed video stores full pictures, called keyframes, only every few seconds and records changes in between. A cut without re-encoding can only start cleanly on a keyframe, so the clip begins at the nearest one, sometimes a couple of seconds early. Switch to Precise mode if the exact first frame matters.

Q: Can I cut out a section from the middle of a video?
A: This tool keeps one continuous part of the video. To remove a middle section, trim twice: once to keep the part before it and once to keep the part after it. Joining the two clips back together needs a video editor. For most uses, keeping one highlight clip is enough.

Q: Can I trim a video on my phone?
A: Yes. The trimmer works in modern mobile browsers. Fast mode is quick even on phones because it does not re-encode. Precise mode and very large files are slower on phones and may fail on devices with little memory, so use a computer for long or 4K videos if you can.

Q: Which formats can I trim?

## What a watermark is for

A watermark is a visible label across your pages. It does three useful jobs:

- **Signals status**: "DRAFT" tells everyone this is not the final version; "SAMPLE" or "SPECIMEN" stops a document being mistaken for an original.
- **Signals ownership**: a faint company logo on a proposal or a design portfolio shows where it came from.
- **Limits reuse of copies**: a line such as "Submitted to XYZ Bank for home loan, 02-11-2026" across an ID copy makes it awkward to reuse for something else.

What a watermark is not: a lock. Anyone with editing software may manage to remove or cover it. Treat it as a strong label and deterrent, and control who receives the file for real security.

## How to add a watermark step by step

1. Open [Watermark PDF](https://biscsindia.com/tools/watermark-pdf/) and choose your PDF.
2. Choose **Text** or **Image**.
3. For text, type your watermark and set the **Font size** and **Colour**. For an image, choose a PNG or JPG and set its **Width** as a percentage of the page.
4. Choose a **Layout**: Center, Diagonal (corner to corner) or Tiled (repeated across the page). For Center and Tiled, you can set the rotation angle.
5. Adjust **Opacity**. The default is 30%.
6. In **Pages**, leave it empty for all pages or type a range.
7. Check the preview, then apply and download.

## Choosing the right layout

| Layout | Effect | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| Diagonal | One large mark from corner to corner | DRAFT, CONFIDENTIAL, COPY |
| Center | One mark in the middle at the angle you choose | Logos, subtle branding |
| Tiled | The mark repeats across the whole page | ID copies, design proofs, documents likely to be cropped |

Tiled is the hardest to crop out, which is why it suits identity documents and creative work shared for review.

## Watermarking ID copies before sharing

India runs on photocopies of identity documents: Aadhaar for a SIM card, PAN for a bank account, a driving licence for a car rental. Once shared, those copies can travel further than you intended.

A common, sensible habit is to write the purpose and date across the copy. With this tool you might use the text "For SBI savings account KYC only – 02 Nov 2026" in Tiled layout at 20–25% opacity. Keep it light enough that the recipient can still read the details they legitimately need. If the copy came from DigiLocker as a PDF, you can watermark it directly; if it is a photo, convert it first with [Images to PDF](https://biscsindia.com/tools/jpg-to-pdf/).

Some organisations have their own rules about what a copy must show, so if a watermarked copy is rejected, ask what they require.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- **Opacity too high.** A dark, solid watermark can make the document unreadable, defeating its purpose.
- **Covering key details.** On forms and ID copies, make sure names, numbers and photos remain visible.
- **Watermarking before final edits.** The watermark is part of the page once saved. Finish editing, page ordering and numbering first.
- **Using Indian-language text.** Text watermarks use a standard font that covers English and Western characters only; unsupported characters become "?". Use an image watermark for other scripts.
- **Relying on it as security.** For truly sensitive files, share less: remove unnecessary pages instead of only marking them.

## Text watermark ideas

- DRAFT, or DRAFT v2, for documents under review.
- CONFIDENTIAL, or INTERNAL USE ONLY, for office reports.
- SAMPLE, or SPECIMEN, for templates and demo invoices.
- PAID, or CANCELLED, for internal record copies of invoices.
- Your name and the recipient for review copies of creative work, for example "Shared with Ravi, preview only".

## Tips for a clean logo watermark

- Use a PNG with a transparent background, so only the logo appears and not a white box.
- Start with a width of about 30–40% of the page for a centred logo.
- Lower the opacity to around 15–20% so it reads as a background element.
- Pair it with [Add Page Numbers](https://biscsindia.com/tools/pdf-page-numbers/) for proposals that need both branding and numbering.

## Example: sending a draft agreement for review

A startup in Kolkata is circulating a draft vendor agreement to three partners. To avoid anyone signing an outdated version, the founder adds "DRAFT – NOT FOR SIGNATURE" in the Diagonal layout at 25% opacity, in grey. When the final version is agreed, the clean, unwatermarked file is the one sent for signing with [Sign PDF](https://biscsindia.com/tools/sign-pdf/).

## Watermark before or after other steps?

Order matters, because a watermark becomes part of each page once it is saved.

1. Edit content, fill forms and fix any typos first.
2. Arrange, merge, remove or rotate pages.
3. Add page numbers if needed.
4. Add the watermark.
5. Compress last, if the file is too large to send.

If you watermark first and then remove a page, nothing breaks, but if you watermark and then need to edit the wording underneath, you will be working around the mark. Keeping a clean, unwatermarked master copy on your device avoids that problem entirely: you can always produce a fresh watermarked copy for each recipient.

## Privacy

Watermarking is often done precisely because a document is sensitive, so it would be odd to upload it to a stranger's server to do it. This tool stamps the pages inside your browser and saves the result to your device. Nothing is sent anywhere.

Q: Should I watermark copies of my Aadhaar or PAN card?

A: A determined person with editing software may be able to remove or cover a watermark, because it is drawn on top of the page. A watermark is a deterrent and a label, not a security lock. For real protection, limit who receives the file.

## Where does messy whitespace come from?

Messy spacing is rarely your fault. Common sources include:

- **PDFs**, where every visual line ends with a hard line break, and columns can add extra spaces.
- **Websites**, which may include non-breaking spaces, zero-width characters and indentation from the page code.
- **Word processors**, where people use tabs or multiple spaces to line things up.
- **WhatsApp and email exports**, which can carry odd spacing and invisible direction marks.
- **Spreadsheets**, where cells often end with a trailing space that breaks lookups and duplicate checks.
- **OCR results** from scanned documents, which frequently include doubled spaces and broken lines.

## How to clean up text online

1. Open the [Whitespace Cleaner](https://biscsindia.com/tools/whitespace-cleaner/).
2. Paste your messy text into the left box, or click **Sample** to see an example.
3. Check the options. The common fixes are on by default.
4. The cleaned text appears on the right, with a badge showing how many characters were removed and how many invisible characters were found.
5. Click **Copy** or **Download** to save the result. **Use as input** lets you run a second pass with different options.

## What each option does

| Option | Default | What it fixes |
|---|---|---|
| Trim each line | On | Spaces at the start and end of every line |
| Collapse multiple spaces | On | "Total  amount   due" becomes "Total amount due" |
| Collapse blank lines | On | Three or more empty lines become one blank line |
| Remove all empty lines | Off | Deletes every blank line, joining paragraphs into one block of lines |
| Remove line breaks | Off | Joins all lines into one continuous paragraph |
| Tabs → spaces | On | Replaces each tab with four spaces (then collapsed if that option is on) |
| Remove invisible characters | On | Zero-width spaces, byte order marks, soft hyphens and control characters |

When **Remove invisible characters** is on, unusual space characters such as non-breaking spaces and the wide ideographic space are also converted to ordinary spaces, so they collapse and trim like normal.

## Fixing text copied from a PDF

This is the most common job. A sentence copied from a PDF often arrives split over three lines: "The applicant must submit the form", then "along with a self-attested copy of", then "the Aadhaar card and PAN card." Pasted into an email or a portal, it looks broken and wastes space.

To turn it back into a flowing paragraph:

1. Paste it into the cleaner.
2. Tick **Remove line breaks**. All lines are joined with single spaces.
3. If the original had several paragraphs, add the paragraph breaks back by hand where needed.

For a long document, it is often quicker to work paragraph by paragraph. If you are starting from the PDF itself, extract the text with [PDF to Text](https://biscsindia.com/tools/pdf-to-text/) first.

## The hidden problem: invisible characters

Invisible characters are the reason two lines that look identical sometimes refuse to match. A zero-width space between "GST" and "IN" is invisible on screen, but a spreadsheet formula, a search box or a duplicate checker sees two different strings.

They cause real problems:

- **Form validation fails.** A PAN or IFSC code copied from a website is rejected as invalid.
- **Duplicates survive.** [Remove Duplicate Lines](https://biscsindia.com/tools/remove-duplicate-lines/) treats "Rahul" and "Rahul" with a hidden character as different names.
- **Code breaks.** A zero-width space in a JSON file or script causes confusing errors.
- **Word counts are off.** Some tools count hidden characters.

The cleaner shows a warning badge with the number of invisible characters it found, which is a useful clue when something "looks right but does not work".

## Common mistakes to avoid

- **Removing line breaks from lists.** If your text is a list, one item per line, do not tick Remove line breaks, or everything becomes one long line.
- **Removing all empty lines from articles.** That merges paragraphs together. Use Collapse blank lines instead.
- **Collapsing spaces in aligned text.** If spaces are used to line up columns, as in some bank statements or code, collapsing them destroys the alignment.
- **Cleaning code without thinking.** In Python and YAML files, leading spaces carry meaning. Untick **Trim each line** for code.

## Tips for common jobs

**Cleaning a spreadsheet column.** Paste the column, keep the defaults on, and paste the cleaned list back. Trailing spaces and hidden characters are gone, so lookups and filters work again.

**Preparing text for a form or portal.** Government and banking portals sometimes reject pasted text with odd characters. A quick pass through the cleaner often fixes "invalid input" errors.

**Tidying chat exports.** WhatsApp exports can contain extra spaces and empty lines. Clean them first, then use [Find and Replace](https://biscsindia.com/tools/find-and-replace/) to remove timestamps or names.

**Before counting words.** Clean the text first, then paste it into the [Word Counter](https://biscsindia.com/tools/word-counter/) for an accurate paragraph and line count.

## Quick checklist after cleaning

Before you paste the result into its final home, take ten seconds to check:

- Paragraphs are still separated where they should be.
- Lists still have one item per line.
- Numbers such as account numbers, mobile numbers and amounts have not been joined to neighbouring words.
- Indentation that matters, as in code or poetry, is still there.
- The "characters removed" badge looks reasonable for what you expected to fix.

If anything went too far, untick the option responsible and the result updates instantly, because the original text is still in the left box.
